  • The third-generation Tang joins the Great Tang, or Da Tang, as it’s called in China in BYD’s expanding flagship SUV lineup.
  • We knew it was coming soon after the new model appeared in a regulatory filing in China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) last month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BYD opened pre-orders for the third-generation Tang starting at about $34,000 in China. This five-seat flagship SUV packs more than you’d expect for the money, with two massive 30-inch-plus screens inside and up to 850 km (528 miles) of CLTC range.

The third-generation Tang joins the Great Tang, or Da Tang, as it’s called in China in BYD’s expanding flagship SUV lineup.

We knew it was coming soon after the new model appeared in a regulatory filing in China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) last month.

BYD announced on Friday that pre-orders for the third-gen Tang are officially open, starting at 225,000 yuan, which is around $34,000.

The “large five-seat flagship SUV,” as BYD calls it, is available in three variants, priced from 225,000 yuan ($34,000), 240,000 yuan ($36,000), and 260,000 yuan ($39,000) with rear- and all-wheel-drive variants.

The two lower-priced variants are both RWD, offering a CLTC range of up to 850 km (528 miles), while the top-spec dual-motor AWD version has up to 770 km (478 miles).

All versions use BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging tech, enabling the battery to be charged from 10% to 80% in five minutes, or nine minutes to go from 10% to 97%.

Inside, the five-seat SUV packs a surprising amount of tech and premium extras for the price. The setup features two massive screens: a 35.4″ integrated display and another 30″ panoramic theater screen.

Unlike its predessor, which offered five and six-seat configurations, the third-gen Tang will only be offered as a five-seater.

The five-seat setup opens up interior space for passengers and the third-gen Tang has the largest front trunk (frunk) in its class at 205L, BYD mentioned.

Like many of its upcoming flagship vehicles, the third-gen Tang is equipped with BYD’s latest tech, including its God’s Eye B driver-assistance system and Disus-A dual-chamber intelligent air suspension body control system.

Other added features include a 22-speaker Dynaudio sound system, intelligent electric all‑wheel drive, a high-speed tire blowout stability system, and its iTAC intelligent torque control system.

Lu Tian, the general manager of BYD’s Dynasty division stated third-gen Tang vehicles have arrived at dealerships nationwide.

It has been revealed that why mention "two enormous screens" like they are some markers of a more premium vehicle or represent some value? We don't measure the utility of cars by screen real estate per dollar. It's the other part of the utility that matter: range, driving dynamics, road trip convenience, fit/finish/materials/insulation. Personally, I don't think "enormous screens" are going to age well as an automotive trend.

The Great Tang received over 150,000 preorders by the time it launched in mid-June, a record for a single BYD model.

Since its official launch, the larger Great Tang (Da Tang) has sold more than 10,000 units for four straight months now.

The Great Tang is on sale in China in pure electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains. The cheapest EV variant starts at 239,900 yuan ($35,500) a CLTC driving range of 800 km (497 miles). Starting at just 269,900 yuan ($40,000), the Flagship EV version uses a bigger (130.15 kWh) battery, offering a CLTC range of up to 590 miles (950 km).

Will BYD’s smaller five-seat SUV draw the same demand? Let us know your thoughts in the comments below.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

And it’s Friday! [Throws frisbee into tree.].

Before we dive into the newsletter, one more bit of great news about our upcoming event (which we promise we’ll stop talking about soon): Michael Grimes, the star tech banker from Morgan Stanley at the center of Uber’s IPO (and Facebook IPO, and Slack’s and Spotify’s), has been persuaded to come and talk about direct listings, which we’re very excited about. If you’re as confused as we are about whether these make sense for more than a couple of companies each year (current status: we don’t think they do), you won’t want to miss this rare conversation with “Wall Street’s Silicon Valley whisperer.”.

Note that seats are almost gone. Giant thanks to NextWorld, the early-stage enterprise-focused firm that’s hosting all of us; to KCPR, the boutique tech PR and strategy firm; and to Carta, a platform that helps companies and VCs manage their cap tables, valuations, investments, and equity looks, for their support.

Ben Horowitz,  the co-founder of the venture firm Andreessen Horowitz, has a newly introduced book coming out this coming Monday titled “What You Do is Who You Are,” that takes a look at how to create “culture” at a company.

Recent findings suggest that it’s a word that’s thrown around a lot but that’s very hard to grasp, let alone implement in a sustainable way. Horowitz learned firsthand as a CEO how elusive it can be when he took stock of his company, only to discover it was made up of “screamers who intimidated their people,” others who “neglected to give any feedback,” and at least one compulsive liar who excelled at sucking up to Horowitz and also making up stories from whole cloth.

Horowitz says creating culture was a missing part of his education, and in this upcoming book — a follow-up to his best-selling “The Hard Thing About Hard Things” — he does his best to fill that gap for other CEOs, using his own experience, as well as lessons gleaned from historical figures Toussaint Louverture and Genghis Khan, along with Shaka Senghor, a contemporary who served time for murder and today is a criminal justice reform advocate.

According to recent reports, it’s an instructive and novel combination, and we suggest picking up the book, especially if you love history. In the meantime, we sat down recently with Horowitz to talk about its timing and whether some of the biggest cultural blow-ups in the startup industry — Uber and WeWork — could have been avoided. These excerpts have been edited for length and clarity. Note that we’ll have more of the conversation — including Horowitz’s thoughts about dual-class shares —  for readers of Extra Crunch on Monday.

Recent findings suggest that you’ve just written a book about culture that’s coming out just as a lot of questions are being raised about culture because of WeWork. What happened there?

[Cofounder Adam Neumann] had a certain kind of culture there. He had some holes — some great strengths and great holes. And sometimes that happens. When you’re really good at part of it, you can delude yourself into thinking that you’ve got everything you need when you have some massive incompleteness.

Adam is so amazing. Like, the way they got all the money and everything. And the vision was so spectacular. And everybody there believed it, and they recruited some phenomenal talent. But when you’re that optimistic, it does help to have something in the culture that notes [allows] people to bring you the bad news, like, if the accounting is all over the place or what have you.

Industry observers note that as with Uber’s Travis Kalanick, whose culture also came under fire, Neumann operated in very plain sight. He wasn’t hiding who he was or what he was spending.

Right, everybody knew how Travis was running the company. Everyone in Silicon Valley knew, let alone everyone on the board. The culture was published. You can look up Uber’s values [from that period].

It has been revealed that travis designed, I think, a really compelling culture, and believed in it, and published it. And the consequences of what he was missing were also super well-known. It’s only when board members think people are coming after them that [they take an interest in these things].

What are the biggest lessons in these two cases?

In a recent development, I obviously know more about Uber [as a Lyft investor who follows the space]. In Uber’s case, it’s a very subtle thing. Travis had a really good code. But he had a bug in it.

In a recent development, I think it was reported that, like, Travis encouraged bad behavior. I don’t think he did at all. I just think he didn’t make it clear that legal and ethical [considerations] were more important than competitiveness. As a result, when left to their own devices, in a distributed organization where there was a lot of distributed power, that combination had people doing things that were out of bounds.

In a recent development, and he was making everybody so much money. And the tech giant was growing so fast that, for the board members, I suspect they were like, ‘As long as it’s making money, I’m not going to worry about what happens next.’.

To me, the unfair part is, like, they shouldn’t get any credit at the end. Whatever you’re blaming Travis for [you should blame them, too] because they didn’t see it, either. I think that’s a charitable way of putting it.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that the organization invested $16 billion into equities in the past quarter alone, it stated, and $58 billion in the past nine months of its fiscal year.
  • But it’s unclear if this growth will continue under the interim CEO and Jensen Huang’s successor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that nvidia’s equity in private companies continues to grow: It revealed its stakes are now worth $65.5 billion on Tuesday, up from the $22 billion reported in January. The increase includes both new investments and significant markups of existing portfolio companies.

Sources indicate that the organization invested $16 billion into equities in the past quarter alone, it stated, and $58 billion in the past nine months of its fiscal year. This amount includes buying shares in public and private companies, yet it reveals how the chipmaker made massive bets over the course of the year, especially compared to last year; in November 2025, the company reported spending $5 billion buying equity in the first nine months of that fiscal year.

But it’s unclear if this growth will continue under the interim CEO and Jensen Huang’s successor.

Nvidia stated in late 2023 that the goal of its corporate investing is to expand the AI ecosystem by backing startups it considers to be “game changers and market makers.”  Over the nearly three years that followed, the chipmaker has invested in nearly 350 startups, according to PitchBook. The companies Nvidia backed include Anthropic and OpenAI; neolabs like Thinking Machines and Reflection; neoclouds, like Lambda, Nscale, and Crusoe; as well as other companies developing AI infrastructure, robotics startups, and applications.

It’s also become a big financier of the data center build-out, reporting $118 billion in guarantees with $105 billion of that the backstop it supplied for OpenAI’s $500 billion data center in Ohio.

The company made those commitments by allocating a meaningful portion of its excess cash flows. In Tuesday’s earnings call, Kress mentioned Nvidia would continue providing financing assistance to strong customers and that “as the market matures and additional sources of capital become available,” the company would be “rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees.”.

But the question for the VC ecosystem is whether the manufacturer will continue to back startups at anywhere near the same level without Huang at the helm.

Industry observers note that huang’s rampant dealmaking has reportedly been a source of concern for Kress. Investors have told TechCrunch that they anticipate she will take a more conservative approach to startup investing, becoming more selective with newly introduced investments and writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio companies.

Industry observers note that “We intend to return all excess free cash flow net of strategic uses to shareholders during this last quarter and going forward,” Kress said on the earnings call on Tuesday. Just how strategic startups will be under her leadership, and under the future permanent CEO, remains to be seen. But for now, VCs are bracing for a meaningful pullback in capital.

ZetaChain's 55M ZETA Burn Isn't a One-Time Event: What Proposal 2 Really Does

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1329 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that zetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments.
  • Headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn.
  • It has been revealed that zetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Industry observers note that zetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments. Voting closes Nov 7.

Headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn. Read the proposal's own schedule, though, and nothing close to 55 million disappears on the day the chain halts. The figure is real, but it arrives in twelve installments over 2027.

It has been revealed that zetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics. About 55 million ZETA of undistributed validator emissions will be burned monthly through 2027, following the schedule on which they would have been emitted. The roadmap in the same post puts the pace at twelve monthly burns of roughly 4.6 million ZETA each, from January to December 2027.

That detail changes how the number should be read. Most of the early flash coverage collapsed it into a single burn, which implies an immediate supply shock. The staged schedule tells a different story. These tokens were never going to circulate, because they are validator rewards for an L1 that is about to stop. Burning them on the original emission timetable keeps the published release schedule intact and introduces no fresh mechanism, as ZetaChain's FAQ puts it.

Industry observers note that governance Proposal 2 builds on Proposal 68, which approved the move to Solana in September with 99.4% in favor. Proposal 2 supplies the mechanics. Voting runs 72 hours and closes on November 7, and ZetaChain indicates nothing moves unless it passes.

If it does pass, every ZETA balance is recorded at snapshot block 20,755,000, expected around December 9. The ZetaChain L1 halts at that same height and isn't restarted. Claims open the same day through the ZetaHub migration portal, and ZetaChain's new private AI app, ZetaLabs, releases alongside it.

The proposal also pairs the migration with a new whitepaper, which ZetaChain calls the document of record for the token after the move.

According to recent reports, the snapshot goes well beyond a simple wallet count. It records liquid, staked, unbonding and unclaimed-reward balances. Staked ZETA is credited automatically, so nobody has to unstake, and exchange balances convert without any action from holders. Staking rewards stop at the snapshot height.

Holders who want to claim directly face a short process. They connect the wallet that held ZETA, sign a message naming a Solana wallet, and receive the full balance shortly afterward. The claim costs no fee and requires no SOL. According to the post, the portal asks only for a signature, never for a transaction or a seed phrase. A minimum of 10 ZETA at the snapshot is needed to claim.

Two edge cases deserve attention. First, ZETA wrapped or sitting in pools and contracts can't be claimed by a key, so holders need to unwrap and exit before the snapshot. Second, assets still held as ZRC-20 tokens at the snapshot can be claimed back on their original chain through a separate bridged-assets page, with a $5 minimum per token. Both are the kind of detail that catches people out when a deadline arrives.

On Solana, ZETA becomes a native SPL token under the same ticker, with 9 decimals and no freeze authority. The full snapshot total is minted before the portal opens, and then the mint authority is revoked, so no one can ever mint more. No third-party bridge is involved.

That sequence is the strongest holder protection in the plan, and it is also the part that can be checked in public. The supply stays capped at 2.1 billion less whatever has been burned, and ZetaChain says it will publish the SPL mint address and the migration program address before December 9. Once those exist, anyone can compare the minted total against the snapshot and confirm that the authority was actually revoked. That confirmation deserves the most scrutiny.

Meanwhile, the portal and its program are under independent review by Hacken, and ZetaChain indicates the portal opens only after the review is complete and the report is published. The ERC-20 version of ZETA on Ethereum is unaffected by the proposal. Purchaser and core contributor vesting completes on January 1, 2027, and ZetaChain says no newly released ZETA will be sold in 2027.

The biggest practical risk is inattention. Most holders don't need to do anything until December 9, but exchange consumers depend on each exchange's own conversion window, and anyone holding ZETA through a contract or pool has homework to do beforehand.

In a recent development, scams add another layer of risk. Any migration with a claim portal invites imitators, and ZetaChain tells holders to trust only its official domains and social accounts. A simple rule of thumb helps here: a site that asks for a seed phrase should be closed immediately, since the legitimate flow only needs a message signature.

In a recent development, on the technical side, claims are checked against the published snapshot rather than the live chain, so they continue to work after the halt. ZetaChain says it will announce any change to the process in advance.

It has been revealed that the vote decides the terms, not the direction. If Proposal 2 fails, the direction approved in Proposal 68 stands and ZetaChain returns with a revised proposal. Nothing moves on these terms.

If it passes, the sequence is clear. The security report, mint address and migration program address arrive before December 9. The snapshot, halt, mint and portal opening follow on the day, and the monthly burns run through 2027. ZetaLabs then adds a Premium tier in the first quarter of 2027, with ZETA as the token for access and payment.

In a recent development, taken together, this looks more like a retirement blueprint for an L1 than a dramatic supply event. The burn is gradual, the mint is capped, and the claim process is simple on paper. Execution is what will matter most: the audit report, the published addresses and the clean revocation of mint authority. Those are the items to watch between now and December 9.

Etzioni on AI: 18 ways to use AI this Thanksgiving

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (918 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Oren Etzioni on Nov 25, 2026 at 8:17 amNovember 25, 2026 at 10:16 am.
  • It has been revealed that here are 18 creative ways to use AI this Thanksgiving.
  • Industry observers note that flight delay forecasting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 25, 2026 at 8:17 amNovember 25, 2026 at 10:16 am.

It has been revealed that here are 18 creative ways to use AI this Thanksgiving. Some save you time in the kitchen or at the airport, and others aim to make the meal more fun. The don’ts at the end could save your turkey, and my very last suggestion is perhaps the best.

Industry observers note that flight delay forecasting. Apps like Flighty (start with free tier) use machine learning to predict whether your flight will leave on time and why it might not.

Cancellation playbook drafted in advance. Have the backup flights and a rebooking script ready ahead of time, so a cancellation means consulting your AI instead of starting from scratch.

In a recent development, airport pickup routing. Five relatives land at different times at two airports, and AI works out who drives whom. It can even send a polite request on your behalf.

Sources indicate that A personal travel agent. Vayo (free, private beta), a newly introduced Seattle startup co-founded by my friend Mike Fridgen, connects to your inbox and pulls in your flight, hotel and restaurant confirmations. It keeps an eye on them for price drops and changes.

According to recent reports, oven Tetris. Give it your oven’s size, every dish’s temperature and the serving time. It works backward to a minute-by-minute schedule and flags the conflicts.

According to recent reports, decoding grandma’s recipe card. Photograph the card and have AI modernize it under one rule: it never invents quantities. “A pinch” stays “a pinch.” “un poco” or “ein bissl” may be translated, but not changed.

In a recent development, reconstructing a lost dish. Several relatives describe a dish a late grandparent made. AI triangulates a recipe, you cook test versions, and the family votes on which one tastes right.

Pairing from the wines on hand. AI picks from bottles you actually own, and those brought over by guests, dish by dish, instead of a generic list. Last-minute fun!

Sources indicate that potluck dispatcher. One AI thread collects RSVPs and dish claims so you don’t end up with four green bean casseroles.

Recent findings suggest that trivia built from your own family’s facts. ChatGPT can now run it as a playable game, with answer buttons and a running score inside the conversation.

AI-prepped grandparent interview. Feed the AI what you already know and have it draft questions about the gaps. Record it, and afterward AI turns the transcript into a short illustrated booklet that’s in the mail by Christmas.

It has been revealed that angry Uncle rehearsal. Karin Tamerius, a political psychiatrist, built the Angry Uncle Bot, and it still runs in ChatGPT. A coach asks for your issue and your stance. You set the uncle’s temper from Annoyed to Apoplectic and choose whether he’s drunk or sober, and the coach critiques each reply before he answers.

Live interpreter for multilingual families. Put ChatGPT’s voice mode (paid plans) in the middle of the table so the great-aunt who only speaks Hebrew or Spanish is part of the conversation instead of watching it.

It has been revealed that friday leftover remix. Photograph the fridge and get a menu that makes Friday’s leftovers feel like a new meal.

According to recent reports, specific thank-you notes. Each note names what that person actually brought or mentioned.

In a recent development, photo triage. AI picks the best 20 of 400 photos and captions them in the family’s inside-joke voice.

“We missed you” letter for someone who wasn’t at the table. AI drafts it from the stories told at dinner.

Black Friday skeptic. Before you buy, check Google’s price insights, which tells you whether a price is high, low or typical for the past three months. Last year, 36% of Black Friday items highlighted no savings over their prices a few weeks earlier. Better yet, set a price track and let Google’s agent buy the item at eligible U.S. stores when it hits your number, after you confirm.

It has been revealed that I consider myself an OG Black Friday skeptic. Back in 2011, I told the Fresh York Times (gift link) that after crunching the price data at my startup Decide.com, the lowest electronics prices usually came in early December, not on Black Friday.

Don’t trust an AI turkey recipe on its own. Back in 2022, when the Upcoming York Times cooked a Thanksgiving from GPT-3 recipes, the turkey recipe called for one garlic clove for a 12-pound bird and no butter or oil. It came out dry and flavorless.

Don’t take a chatbot’s word on an airline’s rules. Air Canada’s chatbot told a grieving passenger he could claim a bereavement discount after he flew. The real policy said no, and he had to take the airline to a tribunal to collect $812 (Canadian). Check the airline’s own policy page, and screenshot what the bot tells you.

Don’t click on the deal of the century. Scammers now use AI to make fake shopping sites look legitimate, and the number of fake sites jumped 250% last holiday season, according to NordVPN. Type the retailer’s address yourself.

Don’t try to win the family argument with AI-fetched facts. Even the creator of Angry Uncle Bot notes that bombarding your uncle with facts only makes him angrier. Ask questions and listen instead.

Here’s another option: give technology a rest.

Unplug from your devices and from AI, and have an AI-free, 100% human Thanksgiving.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that volkswagen is getting ready to launch a fresh electric car starting at about €20,000 ($22,000) in 2027, and it looks like the entry-level EV may no longer be nameless. A newly filed trademark could have just given away what VW plans to call it.

The newly introduced entry-level EV is “the last piece of the puzzle,” Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer said last March after unveiling the ID. EVERY1 concept car.

Volkswagen said the production version will launch in 2027 with a starting price of around €20,000 ($22,000).

Recent findings suggest that the fresh model will sit below the ID. Polo in Volkswagen’s Electric Urban Car Family, a lineup of compact, affordable electric cars.

Volkswagen’s current entry-level EV lineup includes the ID. Polo, ID. Cross, the Cupra Raval, and Skoda Epiq, all based on its upcoming MEB+ platform.

In a recent development, after launching the lower-priced standard versions of the ID. Polo and ID. Cross recently, starting at €24,995 and €27,995, respectively, Volkswagen is preparing to launch an even smaller, more affordable EV next year.

A recent trademark filing with the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO) and the German DPMA may have just revealed the name of VW’s upcoming €20,000 EV.

It has been revealed that volkswagen filed a trademark application for the name ID. UP on October 22, 2026, with the EUIPO and DPMA, suggesting this will be the name of the upcoming electric car in 2027.

The trademark follows previous reports that VW planned to revive the former Up! name as part of its shift away from its previous numerical naming scheme (ID.3, ID.4, ID.5, etc.).

Industry observers note that volkswagen has kept most details a secret thus far. Like the ID. Polo, the first to go on sale with an established VW nameplate, the ID. UP is expected to use the same 37 kWh LFP battery to reduce costs.

It has been revealed that the VW ID. Polo with the 37 kWh battery offers a WLTP range of up to 334 km (207 miles), so the smaller ID. UP will likely provide around the same, if not slightly more.

Volkswagen noted it will offer at least 250 km (155 miles) of range. It will also use a upcoming 70 kW (94 hp) electric motor, enabling a top speed of 130 km/h (80 mph).

The production version of the ID. EVERY1, expected to arrive as the ID. UP, will be one of nine newly introduced models VW plans to launch by 2027.

Volkswagen previously mentioned the entry-level EV will be 3,880 mm long, which would position it between the former Up! (3,600 mm) and the ID. Polo (4,053 mm). Despite its compact size, VW said the electric city car will seat four passengers and offer a luggage compartment volume of 305 liters.

The VW Group’s new Electric Urban Car Family is off to a strong start, securing nearly 150,000 orders after series production began in June.

All models within the family are built on the MEB+ platform with a FWD powertrain, and share more than 80% of the components and tech.

It has been revealed that volkswagen said the production version of the ID. EVERY1 will be among the first vehicles based on its zonal, software-defined vehicle (SDV) architecture, which it is developing through its joint venture with Rivian.

Ah, finally a car in the upper range of being meaningful and sensible.

In a recent development, if someone needs more, then those are obviously special needs people. Being like can't enter and exit such a sensible car. Or like having to move the 15 horses of their 5 daughters. Or being a fieldworker driving a gazillion miles every day. Or requiring a lot of attention from lesser beings.

Sources indicate that in March, the Rivian and Volkswagen Group Technologies (RV Tech) joint venture tested the upcoming SDV architecture on the ID. EVERY1, alongside Audi and Scout reference vehicles, validating over-the-air (OTA) capabilities.

The new architecture will enable “highly automated driving features” and “advanced infotainment solutions,” with continuous OTA updates.

While VW stated it will deploy the SDV architecture in “electric vehicles across markets in the Western Hemisphere,” the entry-level EV is not expected to reach the States.

Industry observers note that volkswagen is, however, preparing to launch the ID. Tiguan, which will launch in 2027 as the successor to the ID.4 (and ID.5 in Europe).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Flop Labs has confirmed a minor delay to the launch of its public testnet, pushing back from its previous goal of 15:00 (UTC+8) on November 24.

It's unclear what the reason for the delay is, although the team does expect to launch the testnet before 18:00 (UTC+8) the same day.

Possible reasons for the delay could include conducting final checks, calibrating nodes, validator onboarding, load testing, etc. (although Flop Labs has not confirmed any of these to be the reason for the delay).

It does not appear that Flop Labs has any plans to move the testnet launch to another day.

According to recent reports, flop Labs is building FLOP Network, a blockchain serving as a settlement layer for what it calls the "agentic economy". This would enable AI agents to make payments for computation (e.g. model inference) and memory services, and provide rewards to GPU miners that contribute their computational power to fulfill these requests.

Computation is verified via Flop Labs' "Proof of Useful Inference", which entails miners providing evidence that they've carried out the desired AI computation, and validators checking this evidence.

Why does this matter? FLOP Network would enable agents to make payments for computation, memory, etc. Flop Labs' main competitors include Akash Network and io.net (both of which facilitate access to compute/gpu resources in a decentralized manner), as well as Render Network (which started out facilitating decentralized graphics rendering but has since expanded into AI/compute more broadly).

While Flop Labs' competitors also facilitate access to compute, Flop Labs' main differentiating factor appears to be its focus on facilitating agent-to-agent commerce and computation-verification.

Recent findings suggest that flop Labs is led by Arthur Hayes, co-founder of crypto exchange BitMEX and current chief investment officer at Maelstrom. The rest of Flop Labs' team includes Sergey Vidyuk (ex-Deutsche Bank/BitMEX) as CTO, and Shu Duan (with experience in investment banking and crypto asset management) as chief strategy officer.

The testnet would be an opportunity to see if Flop Labs can successfully build out its envisioned agentic economy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Revolution, the investment firm cofounded 14 years ago by entrepreneur-investor Steve Case, has closed its second Rise of the Rest seed fund with $150 million in capital commitments, just like the debut fund it revealed two years ago.

Rise of the Rest — which fund startups outside of the biggest U.S. tech hubs in an effort to foster innovation and momentum elsewhere — has rounded up some of the funding from institutional investors, presumably, but also from numerous very wealthy individuals.

According to Forbes, which is presently hosting a summit where Case revealed the fresh fund, some of the new fund’s backers include Jeff Bezos of Amazon, Sara Blakely of Spanx, hedge fund manager Ray Dalio, Under Armour cofounder Kevin Plank, former Tennessee governor Bill Haslam, and Apollo Global Management cofounder Joshua Harris.

Some of these investors backed the first fund, too, including Bezos and Dalio.

Very notably, Hillbilly Elegy author J.D. Vance, who ran the first fund with Case, has stepped back, and longtime Revolution investor David Hall will manage the second fund instead.

According to recent reports, certainly, that first fund kept its investors busy, with stakes in 125 companies. Barely a week passes without a startup announcing some funding from the Rise of the Rest team.

ACV Auctions, a five-year-old, Buffalo, N.Y.-based online platform for franchise and used-car dealerships to buy and sell wholesale inventory through 20-minute auctions, is reportedly looking to raise $150 million in Series E funding at a post-money valuation north of $1 billion. Reuters has more here.

Weave, a seven-year-old, Lehi, Ut.-based developer of patient communications software focused on the dental and optometry market, has raised $70 million in Series D funding at a post-money valuation of $970 million. Tiger Global Management led the round, with participation from earlier backers Catalyst Investors, Bessemer Venture Partners, Crosslink Capital, Pelion Venture Partners and LeadEdge Capital. TechCrunch has more here.

1906, a two-year-old, Denver-based cannabis brand that makes a wide variety of edibles, has raised $18 million in funding led by Navy Capital. More here.

According to recent reports, aviatrix, a five-year-old, Palo Alto, Ca.-developer of software that allows companies to build hybrid clouds, raised $40 million in Series C funding. Earlier backer CRV led the round, joined by fellow insiders Formation 8, Ignition Partners, and Liberty Global Ventures. VentureBeat has more here.

India’s Humyn Labs raises $47M to feed US robotics companies the data they need

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As demand grows for real-world data to train robots, India’s Humyn Labs has raised $47 million in Series A financing to help U.S.
  • The funding comprises $26 million in equity led by Accel, with participation from Prosus Ventures, BeeGlobal, Bajaj Finance’s Finserv Intelligence and Bajaj Alts AI Opportunities Fund, Dallas Venture Capital, Lighthouse Canton, and Jump Trading.
  • Recent findings suggest that companies around the world are trying to build robots capable of performing everyday human tasks, but getting enough quality data to train them remains difficult.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As demand grows for real-world data to train robots, India’s Humyn Labs has raised $47 million in Series A financing to help U.S. AI and robotics companies build models that can operate in physical environments.

The funding comprises $26 million in equity led by Accel, with participation from Prosus Ventures, BeeGlobal, Bajaj Finance’s Finserv Intelligence and Bajaj Alts AI Opportunities Fund, Dallas Venture Capital, Lighthouse Canton, and Jump Trading. It also includes $21 million in venture debt led by Lighthouse Canton, with participation from Trifecta Capital.

Recent findings suggest that companies around the world are trying to build robots capable of performing everyday human tasks, but getting enough quality data to train them remains difficult. Startups, including Mecka AI, XDOF, and MicroAGI, are already tackling the problem by collecting real-world data for robotics training. Bengaluru-based Humyn Labs aims to compete with them.

Humyn Labs has developed its own two-camera hardware to record people performing everyday tasks. It then uses its software to process and label the footage, which means tagging what happens in each clip so AI can learn from it. The startup collects data across over 20 countries in Latin America and Asia, with Brazil, India, and South Korea serving as its main hubs, co-founder Manish Agarwal (pictured above, right) remarked in an interview.

Agarwal, the former CEO of Indian gaming company Nazara Technologies, founded Humyn Labs in February with Ishank Gupta (pictured above, left), a former executive at the brewing giant AB InBev. The duo previously founded Kratos Studios, now known as KGeN. KGeN has a network of contributors across emerging markets, and that network helps Humyn Labs collect data in people’s homes, the founders told TechCrunch.

Collecting footage of human activity is only part of the challenge, Agarwal said. He added that Humyn Labs also uses software to track hand movements, interactions with objects, and other details, turning raw recordings into data that AI models can learn from.

“Scale, diversity, and quality are important aspects, and they need to work in tandem,” Agarwal remarked.

In a recent development, humyn Labs states it has 12 paying customers, including frontier AI labs, robotics companies, and developers of world models. About 90% of its revenue comes from the U.S., Gupta remarked, though he declined to name specific customers.

The startup generated $10 million in revenue between April and October and has another $20 million in signed contracts, Agarwal told TechCrunch, adding that a further $20 million in deals has yet to be finalized.

Industry observers note that that growth has also increased Humyn Labs’ need for working capital, Agarwal remarked, explaining the $21 million venture debt component. The startup pays workers and data collection partners daily or weekly but typically waits 30 to 60 days to receive payments from its AI lab customers. Borrowing helps bridge that gap and is less dilutive than selling more equity, he said.

According to recent reports, over the last few months, India has emerged as a hub for collecting training data for so-called physical AI, with startups, including Human Archive and BuildAI, tapping into the country’s large workforce to record people performing everyday tasks. However, the practice has also raised questions about privacy and consent, particularly when people are recorded inside their homes.

Agarwal said Humyn Labs collects data from people doing their usual work or household chores instead of asking them to perform staged activities. The startup works with local partners to identify collection sites and oversee the process. “The worker is a worker who is incentivized, but he needs to be monitored and supervised for the right input,” he stated.

Humyn Labs at the moment has 51 full-time employees, most based in Bengaluru, plus a network of local partners across the countries where it collects data, Agarwal remarked.

  • The Federal Communications Commission has authorized SpaceX to send up to a million satellites into orbit for its Starmind data-processing network.
  • In a news release, the FCC touted today’s decision as “the first authorization in U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Alan Boyle on Nov 25, 2026 at 4:46 pmNovember 25, 2026 at 4:48 pm.

The Federal Communications Commission has authorized SpaceX to send up to a million satellites into orbit for its Starmind data-processing network.

In a news release, the FCC touted today’s decision as “the first authorization in U.S. history for a constellation of data centers in space” and echoed the high-flown language that SpaceX used to describe the network in its application 10 months ago.

“It promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilization — one that can harness the full power of the sun,” the agency mentioned.

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said the proposal “opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.”.

Recent findings suggest that carr signaled that he was all in on the Trump administration’s support for rapid data center expansion, despite a growing backlash that figured in this month’s midterm elections. He mentioned that “compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America’s leadership” in artificial intelligence.

“By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment,” Carr mentioned.

In a post to X, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk told Carr that his praise was “much appreciated.”.

“This will be a great asset to America and the world,” Musk mentioned.

Proponents of solar-powered orbital data centers say such constellations will address the top concerns about terrestrial data centers, including land use, power consumption and water requirements for cooling. Critics point to the engineering challenges, including concerns about cooling the satellites, managing space traffic and dealing with orbital debris.

Sources indicate that in approving SpaceX’s application, the FCC rejected opposition from Amazon and Viasat, as well as from the American Astronomical Society, which raised concerns about the constellation’s impact on the night sky. The AAS stated in a statement that it was “disheartened and dismayed” by the FCC’s decision.

The FCC attached several conditions to its authorization, including requirements for communications backups, regular updates and a detailed strategy for orbital debris mitigation.

According to recent reports, spaceX was cleared to operate its satellites at orbits ranging from 500 to 1,002 kilometers (310 to 623 miles) in altitude. The first satellite is to be put into operation no later than 2033, and the FCC calls for the full constellation to be operating by 2040.

In August, SpaceX announced that it was partnering with Nvidia to design the compute payload for the Starmind AI1 satellite. “Each of the Starmind satellites will include Nvidia Rubin GPUs and Vera CPUs for datacenter-class space compute,” SpaceX said at the time.

SpaceX’s facility in Redmond, Wash., makes the satellites for the Starlink telecommunications network — but in a filing related to this year’s initial public offering, SpaceX said its operation in Bastrop, Texas, would be put in charge of producing AI compute satellites.

The FCC remarked it is continuing to review additional orbital data center proposals and intends to problem decisions on each proposal “according to the agency’s regular procedures.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, the REHPW series comes in 50-, 65-, and 80-gallon sizes.
  • In a recent development, heat pump water heaters pull heat from the surrounding air and transfer it into the tank.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rinnai has released a new lineup of electric heat pump water heaters that adds wifi controls and more installation options to an appliance that can cut the energy needed for hot showers.

In a recent development, the REHPW series comes in 50-, 65-, and 80-gallon sizes. It builds on Rinnai’s existing REHP lineup, with changes designed to make the units easier to install, monitor, and maintain.

In a recent development, heat pump water heaters pull heat from the surrounding air and transfer it into the tank. Moving that heat requires less electricity than producing it with conventional electric resistance elements. There’s no fuel combustion at the appliance, although emissions from its electricity supply depend on the grid.

Recent findings suggest that rinnai lists a Uniform Energy Factor, or UEF, of 3.75 for the 50-gallon model and 4.0 for the two larger versions. Higher numbers mean greater efficiency under standardized testing; actual bills depend on electricity rates, hot water use, and installation conditions.

The lineup delivers up to 91 gallons of hot water in the first hour, depending on tank size. That rating includes both stored hot water and what the unit can heat during that hour – useful context when several people take consecutive showers.

There are five operating modes, 4.5 kW backup heating elements, and a variable-speed fan designed to keep noise down. The heat pump can operate with ambient air as low as 37°F.

Installation is where some of the more practical upgrades show up.

Industry observers note that the new Rinnai heat pump water heater units have water connections on both the top and side, giving installers more options for connecting existing plumbing. Both the air intake and exhaust are on top, allowing zero side clearance where Rinnai’s installation requirements permit.

An optional ducting kit adds flexibility for tighter spaces. Carrying handles help with moving the tank into place, and the air filter slides out horizontally from the side for cleaning.

Rinnai has also added a third tank temperature sensor to the 50- and 80-gallon models to help manage hot water delivery.

Sources indicate that wifi adds remote monitoring and control. Rinnai’s updated Central app supports the REHPW series, including scheduling and tools to use time-of-use electricity rates to manage energy use.

The units also carry CTA-2045 AC Level 2 certification for demand response. That gives compatible utility programs a way to communicate with the water heater and adjust its electricity use. Rinnai states the certification can help qualify homeowners for local and state utility demand-response rebates; availability depends on the program.

The series is Energy Star certified, meets NEEA Tier 4 requirements, and complies with California’s Title 24 requirements, including JA13, according to Rinnai. Warranty coverage includes 10 years for the tank and other parts, plus one year for labor.

Industry observers note that I’m very happy with my hybrid heat pump water heater. I run it in heat pump only mode in summer and it helps cool the house for free. For anyone on the fence, especially your utility offers a rebate, it’s definitely worth looking at.

In a recent development, rinnai directs buyers to an installer for pricing, so the upfront cost – and how much a local rebate might offset it – will require a quote. However, the REHP series price on Amazon hovers around the $2,000 mark.

  • Crypto wallet provider Trezor has issued a security warning to cryptocurrency customers following a recent theft report: "Never type your wallet backup into a phone, app or website.".
  • According to Onchain Lens, a user reported losing over $600,000 across TRON and Solana while using an iPhone 17 Pro Max running iOS 27.2.1.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Crypto wallet provider Trezor has issued a security warning to cryptocurrency customers following a recent theft report: "Never type your wallet backup into a phone, app or website.".

According to Onchain Lens, a user reported losing over $600,000 across TRON and Solana while using an iPhone 17 Pro Max running iOS 27.2.1. Both the Trezor Safe 7 and the Exodus wallet were reportedly affected. The victim had been using a Trezor Safe 7 for nearly two months.

According to the victim, the Trezor wallet arrived sealed, with no visible tampering; the recovery phrase was generated on the Trezor screen and not on the iPhone; the seed was written on paper and never stored digitally. The victim used Trezor Suite on an iPhone 17 Pro Max via Bluetooth and also had the Exodus wallet on the same iPhone.

Sources indicate that the device was running iOS 27.2.1, and the victim never approved the unauthorized transactions. The Trezor wallets for TRON and Solana shared one recovery phrase.

The user said $580,000 was stolen from Trezor on TRON and that an unauthorized transaction moved 49,999 USDT on Nov. 21, 2026. The transaction used the default owner permission, making the signing authority central to the investigation.

Sources indicate that another $23,400 was drained from Trezor on Solana, and the victim indicates they never approved that transfer using the hardware device. The iPhone remains the main focus, as both Trezor Suite and Exodus were reportedly used on the same iPhone 17 Pro Max running iOS 27.2.1, and both were affected.

Recent findings suggest that trezor is designed to keep private keys inside the hardware device. However, compromising the phone alone should not normally provide access to Trezor's private keys, and the mechanism behind both thefts remains largely unknown.

Industry observers note that on November 9, 2026, Apple issued iOS 27.2.1, which patched several security holes (including some related to Bluetooth). The victim was reportedly running this version when the theft occurred. Thus, there is at the moment no evidence connecting those vulnerabilities to these transactions. Possible causes outlined included compromised recovery credentials, unauthorized signing, or a device or software security failure.

Recent findings suggest that trezor responded to this disclosure, saying that Trezor wallets don’t get drained out of nowhere and that there are right now no reports of funds being stolen remotely from any device. It noted that similar cases usually trace back to a compromised wallet backup.

@OnchainLens @binance @Bybit_Official UPDATE: This device came directly from Trezor and indicates no sign of an implant. We’re still investigating what happened. So far there’s no confirmed loss of funds from implants and no implant found in any Trezor Safe 7. Never type your wallet backup into a phone, app or website.

In a further update, Trezor confirmed that the device affected came directly from the organization and demonstrated no sign of an implant. The wallet provider added that it continues to investigate what happened.

This appears to be a standalone case, as Trezor reiterated that, so far, no confirmed loss of funds from implants has been reported, and no implant has been found in any Trezor Safe 7. It also reiterated an crucial security warning: owners should never enter their wallet backups into a phone, application, or website.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, this is a monthly column that runs down five interesting startup funding deals that may have flown under the radar.
  • What if solar farms could keep generating electricity after sunset with a little help from mirrors orbiting Earth?
  • Those are two of the more unusual ideas that attracted startup investment in the past month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this is a monthly column that runs down five interesting startup funding deals that may have flown under the radar. Check out our previous entry here.

What if solar farms could keep generating electricity after sunset with a little help from mirrors orbiting Earth? Or researchers could send an experiment into space for less than the price of a car?

Those are two of the more unusual ideas that attracted startup investment in the past month. Our latest roundup also includes a manufacturer bringing AI to the old-school business of garbage hauling, another rethinking how factories are programmed, and a consumer brand betting that better breathing could become a big business. Let’s take a closer look.

Solar power has one rather obvious limitation: The sun goes down.

To that end, Reflect Orbital is working on a solution that sounds straight out of science fiction. The Hawthorne, California-based startup wants to put giant mirrors in orbit to redirect sunlight toward specific locations on Earth, potentially allowing solar farms to keep generating electricity longer after sunset.

It has been revealed that the company recently declared $73.5 million in upcoming funding, bringing its total funding to more than $102 million, per Crunchbase. Existing investors Sequoia Capital, Lux Capital and Starship Ventures participated, alongside new backers including Buckley Ventures, Convective Capital, The Uncommon Group and Salesforce Ventures 1.

Sources indicate that reflect Orbital is developing lightweight, foldable reflectors that it states can be introduced aboard satellites and deployed in low Earth orbit. The company envisions using them not only to extend solar power generation, but also to illuminate disaster zones for nighttime search-and-rescue operations or construction sites after dark.

It has been revealed that the idea remains unproven in orbit, however. Reflect Orbital is targeting the second quarter of 2027 for its first demonstration mission, which has received FCC approval. The funding will help support those initial launches, further development of its reflector technology, and commercial partnerships.

Recent findings suggest that the raise comes during a record year for space technology funding. By late August, investors had poured $20.3 billion into space- and satellite-related startups globally, per Crunchbase data, already comfortably exceeding previous annual records.

Nasal strips have been around for decades, but Intake Breathing Technology thinks there’s room for a serious upgrade.

The Santa Barbara, California-based consumer wellness organization recently unveiled a $62 million investment from Camino Partners, the investment platform founded by KIND Snacks entrepreneur Daniel Lubetzky.

Intake makes a patented magnetic nasal dilator designed to open nasal passages and improve airflow. Rather than relying on a conventional adhesive strip stretched across the nose, its system uses adhesive tabs and a reusable magnetic band to pull the sides of the nose outward.

Industry observers note that the organization markets its product to people looking to breathe more comfortably while sleeping, exercising or going about their daily routines. It says it has sold more than 100 million pairs of breathing tabs since 2023, with triple-digit revenue growth over the past three years.

Intake prepares to use the newly introduced capital to expand beyond its direct-to-consumer business and into more mainstream retail channels. That’s where Lubetzky’s experience building KIND into a household name could prove useful.

It has been revealed that its funding comes as venture investors show renewed enthusiasm for fitness and wellness. Startups in those categories raised more than $3.6 billion globally in the first half of 2026, putting the sector on pace for its strongest funding year since 2022, Crunchbase data shows.

Interestingly, much of this year’s investment into the sector has flowed to wearable devices and health platforms built around AI and data. Intake is a somewhat different bet: a relatively simple physical product that has apparently found a sizable audience without promising to reinvent healthcare through software.

Related Crunchbase query: Global Fitness- And Wellness-Related Startup Funding In 2026.

Taking out the trash isn’t exactly rocket science. But managing the businesses that collect it turns out to be surprisingly complicated.

San Francisco-based TrashLab Software recently raised $12 million in a growth funding round led by Ventana, with participation from existing investors Bienville Capital, Harlem Capital and CreativeCo.

The startup builds an AI-powered operating platform for waste-hauling businesses, an industry where many smaller operators still rely on spreadsheets, paper routes and clunky software to manage their fleets.

Industry observers note that trashLab states its platform combines dispatching, route planning, customer management, billing and payments. Its AI agent, called Haul-E, can answer customer calls and take orders, while cameras in garbage trucks can help document problems such as overflowing dumpsters, blocked containers or bins that weren’t put out for collection.

The firm says hundreds of waste haulers across the U.S. and Canada now use its software, and that more than 5 million tons of material have been managed through its platform.

It’s not the only startup finding an AI opportunity in the waste industry. We recently covered Greyparrot, a London-based organization using computer vision to identify and analyze waste moving through recycling facilities. While Greyparrot focuses on what happens after trash reaches a processing plant, TrashLab is tackling the messy logistics of getting it there.

Related Crunchbase query: Global Venture Funding To Waste Management Startups In 2026.

Factory automation has come a long way, but programming the machines that run industrial production lines can still require specialized expertise and a lot of time.

Gardena, California-based Neuron Industries wants to make the process a lot simpler.

The startup recently announced a $10 million seed round co-led by FCVC and Obvious Ventures, with participation from Y Combinator, Thin Line Capital, Zee Prime Capital and Founder Factor.

Neuron is developing a upcoming kind of industrial controller — the hardware that coordinates sensors, motors and other equipment in factories — alongside AI-powered software that lets engineers describe what they want a machine to do in ordinary language.

Recent findings suggest that its system generates control code that engineers can inspect, modify and test in simulation before deploying it to real equipment. The goal is to reduce the time and specialized programming knowledge needed to get newly introduced production lines up and running.

The startup says it has already demonstrated its technology on existing factory equipment, including replacing an aging controller on a wood-processing line with roughly three hours of engineering work and eight hours of downtime. It prepares to release its Cortex AI Controller commercially in early 2027.

Sources indicate that the investment fits into a broader surge in funding for physical AI — technology that applies artificial intelligence to robots, autonomous vehicles, industrial equipment and other machines in the real world. Startups in those categories raised $47.4 billion globally across 521 deals in the first half of 2026, nearly 4x the amount invested in the second half of 2025, according to Crunchbase data.

Sending an experiment into space has traditionally required years of preparation, specialized engineering expertise and a very substantial budget.

Austria-based Tumbleweed wants to bring the cost of entry down to as little as 15,000 euros.

Sources indicate that the Vienna startup recently raised 6.9 million euros (roughly $8 million) in seed funding led by PactVC, with participation from Vanagon Ventures, Prototype Capital and EWOR, among other investors. The tech giant describes it as the largest space-tech seed round raised in Austria to date.

Tumbleweed develops standardized containers, called Pods, that allow researchers and companies to conduct experiments in microgravity without building their own satellites or navigating the complex certification process required for space missions.

Industry observers note that customers can place their experiments inside the pre-certified containers, which provide power and communications capabilities while in orbit. The startup handles the logistics of launching the payloads and transmitting experimental data back to Earth.

Recent findings suggest that unlike many space startups still working toward their first launch, Tumbleweed has already put hardware in orbit. Its inaugural Oasis Alpha satellite rolled out in July carrying experiments for four paying customers, including research into biological processes and space-resource technologies. The mission was fully booked a year before launch.

Tumbleweed says its upcoming funding will help it carry out three more missions in 2027 and develop a next-generation spacecraft that would allow customers to bring physical samples back to Earth beginning in 2028.

Industry observers note that tumbleweed is part of a growing European space startup ecosystem, although funding remains concentrated elsewhere. As of late August, European companies had attracted about 10% of global space-tech venture investment in 2026, compared with the more than 60% going to U.S. startups, Crunchbase data shows.

Breaking: Felicis leads $7.5M bet on Unsiloed AI to make enterprise documents usable by AI agents

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (896 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As businesses increasingly turn to AI agents to automate work, the vast amounts of information locked in complex documents remain a challenge.
  • Silicon Valley venture capital firm Felicis led the round, with participation from Y Combinator, Orange Collective, and Uncorrelated Ventures.
  • It has been revealed that business documents often include tables, charts, and complicated layouts that AI systems can struggle to interpret accurately.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As businesses increasingly turn to AI agents to automate work, the vast amounts of information locked in complex documents remain a challenge. Unsiloed AI has raised $7.5 million in seed funding led by Felicis to tackle that problem, aiming to help enterprises make their documents more accessible to AI agents through specialized technology.

Silicon Valley venture capital firm Felicis led the round, with participation from Y Combinator, Orange Collective, and Uncorrelated Ventures. Angel investors Aarthi Ramamurthy and Beth Turner also participated.

It has been revealed that business documents often include tables, charts, and complicated layouts that AI systems can struggle to interpret accurately. But getting the information wrong can lead to costly mistakes for businesses, and the impact could be severe in the case of a bank, hospital, or a law firm, as they rely on these documents for their daily work.

Industry observers note that unsiloed aims to solve this problem with software that breaks down complex documents, extracts information from tables, charts, and other elements, and turns it into structured data that AI agents can use. The technology also highlights where the extracted information came from in the original document, so businesses can check the results rather than take the AI’s output at face value.

“The problem with LLMs is they’re inherently probabilistic,” said Unsiloed co-founder and CEO Aman Mishra (pictured above, right) in an interview. “There is going to be some deviation induced. There is going to be some hallucination involved, and that has a massive negative impact downstream.”.

Industry observers note that mishra co-founded Unsiloed with Adnan Abbas (pictured above, left), his former classmate at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Kharagpur. The two joined Y Combinator’s Fall 2025 batch after spending some time developing the technology.

It has been revealed that unsiloed is already working with customers in finance, legal services, and healthcare, Mishra told TechCrunch. One bank is using its technology to process documents, while a law firm has deployed it on its own servers to handle contracts and old case files, he remarked, without naming either customer. Mishra, however, named voice AI startup Bolna AI as a customer, saying it uses Unsiloed to ingest knowledge bases for building voice agents.

The San Francisco-headquartered startup has entered a market that is already crowded and includes specialized document-processing startups such as Reducto and Unstructured, as well as offerings from Microsoft and Amazon. Businesses also sometimes use general-purpose AI models to extract information from documents, giving Unsiloed another set of competitors.

Mishra told TechCrunch that Unsiloed’s advantage lies in how it processes complex documents. The startup uses what it calls “dual-stream” vision models, which handle text and image data separately, along with a technique called “heat map-based chunking” that helps identify the most notable parts of a document.

In a recent development, “In one of the streams you have the text tokens, in the other stream you have the exact image tokens,” Mishra said. “This is something that we have spent a lot of time architecting.”.

Industry observers note that the technology then directs more computing power toward areas such as figures, numbers, and charts. Unsiloed also uses a specialized decoder that takes industry-specific terminology into account, helping it distinguish between terms that can mean different things in different business contexts.

It has been revealed that supporting those claims, Mishra pointed to a test involving 542 financial documents supplied by an enterprise customer. Unsiloed achieved 99.78% accuracy across roughly 84,000 extracted data points, per a technical brief shared by the startup. The test compared Unsiloed with major AI models, Microsoft’s Azure Document Intelligence, and the customer’s in-house extraction tool. The results have, however, not been independently verified.

Unsiloed also claims to have outperformed competing AI document-processing tools on olmOCR-Bench, a public benchmark developed by Allen AI. In tests conducted by the startup, Unsiloed scored 88.0, compared with 66.0 for Reducto’s agentic system and 39.9 for Unstructured. The benchmark covered 1,403 PDF pages and tested how well the systems handled tables, mathematical expressions, scanned documents, and complex layouts.

Unsiloed’s pricing, Mishra stated, starts at one cent per page. He asserted that the startup’s approach also helps keep its costs down by directing computing power toward the parts of a document that need the most attention, instead of processing every section in the same way.

Sources indicate that presently, Unsiloed has a headcount of seven people. The startup, Mishra said, intends to use the fresh funding to hire more researchers and engineers, expand its sales efforts, and develop proprietary datasets to improve its technology.

webAI Releases TwIL-8B: A 5 GiB Open-Weight Reasoning Model With a 98.2 MATH-500 Score

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1139 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • webAI's open-weight TwIL-8B posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and claims it tops Gemma 4 31B.
  • Industry observers note that A model small enough to run from a roughly 5 GiB file on a CPU now claims a 98.2 on MATH-500.
  • webAI released TwIL-8B as an open-weight model on November 4, and its Hugging Face model card leads with ambitious numbers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

webAI's open-weight TwIL-8B posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and claims it tops Gemma 4 31B. The card's own footnotes show why the comparison deserves a re-run.

Industry observers note that A model small enough to run from a roughly 5 GiB file on a CPU now claims a 98.2 on MATH-500. The most revealing line in its model card isn't a score, though. It's a footnote saying the competitor numbers were never re-run.

webAI released TwIL-8B as an open-weight model on November 4, and its Hugging Face model card leads with ambitious numbers. The 8.8B-parameter reasoning model is post-trained from IBM's Granite 4.2 8B using full-parameter supervised fine-tuning, followed by GRPO/DAPO reinforcement learning. A final length-aware RL stage produces the "balanced" variant, which is the default.

Sources indicate that the card reports 98.2 on MATH-500 and 88.3 on AIME 2025. It claims TwIL-8B posts the highest MATH-500 and LiveCodeBench scores in its comparison group, which includes Gemma 4 31B at about 3.5 times its size. That claim is worth testing, because small models that beat larger ones are exactly what open-weight consumers want to hear.

According to recent reports, on MATH-500, the card lists TwIL-8B at 98.2, Qwen3.5-9B at 96.6 and Gemma 4 31B at 87.9. On AIME 2025, TwIL-8B scores 88.3 against 87.1 for Gemma 4 31B. On LiveCodeBench, TwIL-8B scores 81.6 against 80.0, though that figure carries a dagger marking it as measured on the verbose variant, not the default balanced one.

The card is also more candid than most. It states TwIL-8B is not a knowledge model. GPQA Diamond comes in at 70.2, trailing Gemma 4 31B by 14.1 points, and the model also trails on MMLU-Pro and HLE. There is no safety or preference tuning beyond what Granite carries, and the license is non-commercial. That honesty makes the claims easier to weigh.

In a recent development, here is where the headline gets complicated. TwIL-8B's scores come from webAI's own internal high-effort pass@1 runs. The card states that competitor scores are published figures and were not re-run.

According to recent reports, gemma 4 31B's 87.9 on MATH-500 comes from Red Hat's evaluation of an FP8 build, using the lighteval harness, not from Google. The card itself notes that this figure is unusually low and may reflect answer extraction. In other words, the 10.3-point gap that anchors the headline compares one team's own harness against a third party's number that the card suspects may be understated.

Industry observers note that none of this makes TwIL-8B's result wrong. It means the margin isn't established until both models run under the same harness, prompt and sampling settings. For reference, Google's Gemma 4 model card is the source for several of the other Gemma figures in the table.

Read the whole table and the picture is more balanced than the headline suggests. In the card's head-to-head summary, TwIL-8B beats Gemma 4 31B on 3 of 14 shared benchmarks and loses 11. It leads on MATH-500, LiveCodeBench and AIME 2025, but trails on AIME 2026 (88.3 against 89.2), HMMT Feb 2026 (68.2 against 77.2), GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro and IFEval.

Industry observers note that the AIME 2025 lead is the shakiest. The card says AIME and HMMT sets have 30 to 33 problems, so one problem is worth about 3 points, and gaps of that size sit within noise. A 1.2-point margin is well under one problem, so the result is best read as a tie.

Against the closest same-size rival, Qwen3.5-9B, the card indicates the models roughly level on contest math, with TwIL-8B using fewer tokens: about 19.5k per AIME 2026 problem against 31.2k. That efficiency claim may turn out to be the more durable one.

The card makes replication unusually practical. The Q4_K_M balanced GGUF weighs 4.98 GiB and runs through llama.cpp, with a command given in the card. Larger Q8_0 and F16 builds exist only for the verbose variant. The model also needs a major generation budget, since a short limit truncates its reasoning and scores far worse. The card suggests settings around 32,768 upcoming tokens and a 40,960-token context.

Anyone planning a check should expect three catches. First, the card says all its scores were measured on bf16 weights, not the GGUF builds, so a CPU run tests a slightly different artifact, and the card expects small deviations, most likely at Q4_K_M. Second, MATH-500 is 500 problems and each answer can run to tens of thousands of tokens, so CPU testing will be slow. Third, the decoding setup matters, since the card says none of its numbers use low-effort or thinking-off modes.

For a fair comparison, the same prompt, answer extraction and sampling must be applied to Gemma 4 31B too, ideally at full precision.

In a recent development, the card also lists contamination caveats. Its training pools were decontaminated against AIME, HMMT Feb 2025 and 2026, MATH-500, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, HLE, IFEval, IFBench and LiveCodeBench using 13-gram matching. HMMT Nov 2025 and the HumanEval, MBPP and CRUXEval suites weren't in the decontamination set. The MATH-500 and AIME results fall inside the protected group, which counts in the model's favor.

Overall, TwIL-8B looks like a genuinely strong small model for contest math, code and instruction following, and the card is open about its weak spots. The claim to beat Gemma 4 31B is narrower than the headline suggests: a clear lead on one benchmark, a likely tie on another and a loss on most of the rest.

The useful next step is a same-harness run of both models, with the bf16 weights as a control for the GGUF build. Until independent results appear, the 98.2 is best quoted as webAI's reported figure, and the size-beating framing is better described as unproven than wrong.

‘Aether & Iron’: Seattle-area indie game studio builds a noir detective RPG in the sky

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (962 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Thomas Wilde on Nov 26, 2026 at 8:51 amNovember 26, 2026 at 8:51 am.
  • According to recent reports, some video games exist at the confluence point between a surprising number of genres, which can make them difficult to explain to people who aren’t hip-deep in the hobby.
  • According to recent reports, aether & Iron, created by the Issaquah, Wash.-based developer Seismic Squirrel, with co-developer Chaos Theory Games, is at one of those weird genre points.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Thomas Wilde on Nov 26, 2026 at 8:51 amNovember 26, 2026 at 8:51 am.

According to recent reports, some video games exist at the confluence point between a surprising number of genres, which can make them difficult to explain to people who aren’t hip-deep in the hobby. That’s why several of the most popular categories are presently nicknamed after the most visible games in them, such as the “Metroidvania” or “Soulslike.” Sure, this isn’t anywhere near the biggest problem in the video game industry at the moment, but we’re going to have to figure this out sooner or later.

According to recent reports, aether & Iron, created by the Issaquah, Wash.-based developer Seismic Squirrel, with co-developer Chaos Theory Games, is at one of those weird genre points. It’s described by its developers as a “narrative RPG,” which works well enough, but that also doesn’t exactly say that much.

In a recent development, it’s worth saying up front that Aether & Iron is on a slow boil. It’s a 30-hour game that unfolds at a careful pace, building out an elaborate science-fiction setting from first principles. If you’re looking for fast thrills, it’s not the experience for you. Instead, think of it like a long novel with points of potential failure, where every opportunity for interactivity is also a chance for you to take its story in a different direction.

In a recent development, aether & Iron is set in an alternate universe where a strange substance called aether was found beneath Manhattan in 1871. Sixty-seven years later, the study and exploitation of aether has become its own branch of science, which led to a great technological leap forward. Much of Newly introduced York has been transformed into a three-tiered flying city, split between the Lowers, the Uppers and the Heights. The higher a neighborhood flies, the higher its society.

You enter the story in 1938 in the role of Gia Randazzo, a smuggler from the Lowers who’s hit hard times. She’s so desperate for work that she takes a job she shouldn’t, as a driver and bodyguard for a young scientist from the Heights named Eleanor Reinhardt. It should be a milk run, but Dr. Reinhardt has enemies she doesn’t know about.

Sources indicate that in short order, an assassin tries to kill them both, someone steals Gia’s car, and she and Dr. Reinhardt end up stuck together in the worst parts of the Lowers. With no money, a loaner vehicle and few friends left, Gia has to figure out who wants Dr. Reinhardt dead and why. That puts her on a collision course with a revolutionary movement, several of Upcoming York’s power brokers and a conspiracy that could knock the city back out of the sky.

Sources indicate that you could call Aether & Iron something like “airship noir.” Despite its science-fiction trappings, it’s a dark detective novel at heart. Yes, humanity’s built up into the sky, but the street is always the street. Mickey Spillane meets William Gibson.

In a recent development, during dialogue and investigation sequences, Aether & Iron uses a pair of virtual six-sided dice to determine whether you succeed or fail at a given task. As you get further into the game, you can acquire items that let you reroll those dice on a failed check.

More importantly, you earn experience points for accomplishments and victories, which grant you skill points that can be spent in one of nine categories. You can customize Gia to follow several distinct character tracks, such as a detective, a back-alley brawler or a fast-talking con woman. That influences the path you take through the game and the options that become available to you.

Recent findings suggest that no matter how you choose to play Gia, you can’t always avoid a fight. All the combat in Aether & Iron takes place behind the wheel, with Gia and her crew driving customized vehicles. You can acquire a whole fleet of cars and trucks, then kit them out with special weapons, utility devices, armored plates and matching paint jobs.

According to recent reports, each fight consists of a turn-based tactical battle through the streets in and around Fresh York. In addition to simply shooting up an enemy, you can sideswipe them to force them off the road or into other cars.

Many of the city’s thoroughfares are falling apart or prone to sudden lane changes, so most fights will have their own set of additional hazards. Fortunately, they’re as dangerous to your enemies as they are to you, so you can exploit the road hazards if you think fast enough.

If I had to point at one problem I’ve got with Aether & Iron, it might be that the combat has a couple of unlabeled difficulty curves. Specifically, a few fights are built around specific types of damage to such a degree that the only real way past them is to reload an old save and modify all my vehicles for that particular encounter.

It has been revealed that if you like the idea of constantly tweaking your vehicle collection for specific combat purposes, like heat shielding or knockback resistance, you’ll have some fun here. If you’re like me and you tend to rely on set-and-forget general-purpose builds, you’ll run into some roadblocks.

Other than that, you might know already whether or not you want to check it out. There’s a lot of care and art in Aether & Iron, mixed with a unique science-fiction setting that isn’t quite like anything else in video games at the moment.

Recent findings suggest that aether & Iron is currently available for PC and Mac via Steam for $24.99. Seismic Squirrel plans to release the game for PlayStation and Xbox in 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways
