Tech Report: NEAR’s Inflation Cut: The Math Behind a 5.27% to 3.37% Staking Yield

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1288 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • HSP-029 lowers NEAR’s issuance cap from 2.5% to 1.6% over 24 months.
  • Most headlines on NEAR’s new inflation schedule stop at “2.5% to 1.6%.” Stakers feel a different number.
  • It has been revealed that house of Stake ratified HSP-029 on November 16, after the Security Council’s 14-day veto window passed without a veto.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

HSP-029 lowers NEAR’s issuance cap from 2.5% to 1.6% over 24 months. The cap formula, the epoch step and the yield math show what that does to stakers.

Most headlines on NEAR’s new inflation schedule stop at “2.5% to 1.6%.” Stakers feel a different number. They earn about 5.27% today and will earn roughly 3.37% once the cut finishes, and a single line of arithmetic accounts for the gap.

It has been revealed that house of Stake ratified HSP-029 on November 16, after the Security Council’s 14-day veto window passed without a veto. The proposal touches one parameter, the maximum annual issuance rate, which drops from 2.5% to 1.6% over 24 months. It is the second cut in just over a year, coming after the October 2025 halving from 5%.

According to recent reports, everything else stays put. Issuance still splits 90% to staking participants and 10% to the protocol treasury. There is no latest spending program, no validator subsidy and no automatic trigger that could push issuance back up. The full proposal models 11.8 million NEAR of issuance avoided over two years and 66.1 million over six, measured against leaving the cap at 2.5%.

The schedule is a straight line with no stair steps:.

cap(t) = 2.5% − 0.9% × min(t, 24) / 24.

Recent findings suggest that here t is the number of months since the reduction begins. The 0.9% is the total drop (2.5 minus 1.6), and dividing it by 24 gives a monthly step of 0.0375 percentage points, or 3.75 basis points. The min(t, 24) term caps the ramp at month 24, and the cap sits at 1.6% from there on.

NEAR applies the step every epoch rather than once a month. An epoch lasts about 12 hours, so the cap slips by roughly 0.0006 percentage points each time, far too little to notice on any given day. There are no step dates to mark on a calendar. Sampled every six months, the line looks like this:.

In a recent development, the yield column uses the math in the next section. It drops about 0.08 percentage points a month, evenly, with no cliff.

It has been revealed that new tokens go mostly to stakers, so the staked pool splits the reward, and a smaller pool earns more per token. That gives a working formula:.

gross yield ≈ 0.9 × issuance cap ÷ staking ratio.

The 0.9 is the staker share of issuance. Using the proposal’s figures, 0.9 × 2.5% ÷ 0.4271 comes to 5.27%, where 42.71% is the staking ratio reported when the proposal went to vote. Put in the 1.6% cap and 0.9 × 1.6% ÷ 0.4271 gives 3.37%, the same number the proposal publishes. Anyone can check the headline yields on a calculator.

Recent findings suggest that the formula has two limits. It uses the cap, but realized issuance runs a little lower because transaction fees are burned. HSP-029 measured 2.45% in September, which puts today’s yield near 5.16%. The staking ratio also moves. When more people stake, the same rewards spread over more tokens and yield falls further, and when people unstake it climbs. The 3.37% figure assumes today’s ratio holds.

In a recent development, stakers feel it first. By the proposal’s own math, someone staking 1,000 NEAR ends up with about 20 fewer tokens after two years than if the cap had stayed at 2.5%. The numbers back that up: yield averages about 4.32% across the ramp, roughly 0.95 points under today’s rate for two years.

Sources indicate that holders who don’t stake come out ahead. More than half of NEAR’s supply sits unstaked, and every new token dilutes those holdings. Trimming the cap by 0.9 percentage points trims that dilution by the same amount each year. Stakers give up some reward so that everyone else gives up less value.

Recent findings suggest that validators get an easier path than in 2025, when the halving cut staking rewards from about 9% to 4.75% in a single upgrade. Operators now have 24 months to proposal. NEAR’s analysis finds that most validator revenue comes from commission on delegated stake, so service quality and fee competition shape income more than the issuance rate does.

Recent history explains the setup. When the 2025 halving shipped, an earlier community poll had missed the two-thirds threshold, and critics said the core team pushed the change through anyway. HSP-029 sidesteps that argument by design.

Two separate approvals are required. Token holders voting through veNEAR set the direction, and that vote closed November 2 with 99.96% in favor and none against. Validators then decide on their own whether to adopt the protocol upgrade that makes the cap binding. The author, Sal Ternullo of SVRN, opened discussion on October 7, and the process ran through the Screening Committee and Security Council in public. Raising issuance again would take a upcoming proposal and another round of validator adoption, so nothing can be added quietly later.

Industry observers note that ratification does not change issuance yet. A one-quarter grace period comes first, giving wallets, exchanges, custodians and staking providers time to patch their disclosures. NEAR One then releases the upgrade and validators choose whether to adopt it, with the reduction starting about a quarter after ratification. On schedule, that means a start in early 2027 and a 1.6% cap around early 2029.

Sources indicate that three things are worth tracking. Validator adoption of the upgrade comes first, because the cap stays at 2.5% until enough validators run it. The staking ratio comes next, since it moves yield regardless of the formula. Last are the quarterly transparency reports NEAR has promised, which compare realized issuance with the schedule.

Recent findings suggest that price is a separate question. Lower issuance eases supply pressure, but nothing in it creates demand. The cap will follow its published line down, and yield will follow the cap.

The Shiba Inu ecosystem may be set for a privacy boost, as longtime SHIB community member and developer Mazrael hints at privacy potential coming to the blockchain.

Shiba Inu's privacy potential draws from Oxbow's Privacy Pools, the privacy design coauthored by Ethereum cofounder Vitalik Buterin, which is currently a plug-in in the Ethereum Foundation's Kohaku wallet SDK.Mazrael noted that Shibarium is now ready for Oxbow's Privacy Pools, with the groundwork already being done.

It has been revealed that WOOF 🐶🪖🫡 And it's privacy done the regulation-friendly way. Privacy Pools come from a 2023 paper Vitalik co-wrote: deposits are screened, so stolen funds can't hide in the crowd, while honest users stay private. No KYC, no backdoors, and you can always exit publicly. Two ways to bring it to Shibarium: 0xbow deploys it themselves, or the community deploys the same contracts and runs a relayer. Shibarium is ready either way, and ShibWallet already runs it on testnet 🔥.

The groundwork done on Shibarium (Chain ID 109) includes Cancun opcodes, BN254 pairing support for zero-knowledge proofs, CreateX and Arachnid factories and verified PoseidonT3 and PoseidonT4 contracts at Ethereum addresses.

Recent findings suggest that mazrael shared a GitHub document, "Shibarium (chain 109) support: chain is prepared," which highlighted this fact. Addressed to the Oxbow team was a request: "Hi 0xbow team! We build on Shibarium (chain ID 109) and would love to see Privacy Pools there. We've done the groundwork so a deployment would be as easy as possible, and ShibWallet plans to integrate it through Kohaku from day one.".

In a recent development, mazrael explained that Privacy Pools originated from a 2023 paper Ethereum cofounder Vitalik coauthored: deposits are screened, so stolen funds can't hide in the crowd, while honest customers stay private. No KYC, no backdoors and users can always exit publicly.

Two ways to bring it to Shibarium include 0xbow deploys it themselves, or the community deploys the same contracts and runs a relayer.

For the first option, Mazrael has relayed a GitHub request to the Oxbow team, which is currently showing signs of a green light, with Mazrael remarking that "they did the approval thing when we posted basically.".

Industry observers note that A 0xbow privacy pool deployment for Shiba Inu will bring 'entry point', 'verifiers', and 'PrivacyPoolSimple' for native BONE (Shibarium's gas token). It will also bring 'PrivacyPoolComplex' for SHIB and other ecosystem tokens later.

The Shib ecosystem would become privacy-complian and ShibWallet would integrate it through Kohaku from day one.

Why Does AI Get Simple Questions Wrong? What Google's Humanity's First Exam Highlights

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (825 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You ask an AI model to name the color of the third letter in each word on a neon sign.
  • Google DeepMind built a test for exactly that gap, and the results show how far "usually right" can sit from "reliably right.".
  • Most AI benchmarks ask a model to solve a hard problem once.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You ask an AI model to name the color of the third letter in each word on a neon sign. It gets it right. You ask again, and it slips by one letter. Nothing broke.

The model could do the task. It just did not do it every time. Google DeepMind built a test for exactly that gap, and the results show how far "usually right" can sit from "reliably right.".

Most AI benchmarks ask a model to solve a hard problem once. If it passes, it scores. Google DeepMind's Humanity's First Exam (HFE), released on November 24, 2026, asks something different. Can a model solve an easy task, and slight rewrites of it, every single time?

In a recent development, the prompts are elementary on purpose. They cover counting objects, naming colors, tracking where something moved, basic arithmetic, strict formatting rules and spotting false premises. Humans solve them in about a minute.

One public example: "List the color of the third letter of each word in the neon sign in order, separated by a semicolon." The answer is green; yellow; white; blue; blue.

Two scores explain the whole story:.

According to recent reports, the paper calls the difference the Family Reliability Gap. One slip anywhere in the 16 answers fails the whole family.

According to recent reports, the top five models score 96% to 98% on a single try and 100% on family pass@4. Their family pass⁴ averages only 85.8%. Across all 18 models, the gap runs from 7.6 to 80.1 percentage points.

The bottom row is the sharpest case. That model gets 68.7% of single tries right, yet clears only 18.6% of question families every time. Its family pass@4 is 98.8%, so it could solve nearly every family at least once.

According to recent reports, the math is simple. Say a model is right 90% of the time on each answer, and the answers are independent. Getting 16 in a row right happens about 18.5% of the time (0.9 to the 16th power). That is a rough illustration, not the paper's calculation, but it reveals how small error rates compound.

The paper's own example makes the same point. One model trails the leader by 6.6 points on single tries and by 29.4 points on family pass⁴. On average, about half the shortfall comes from prompts a model always fails. The other half comes from flakiness: right on some runs, wrong on others.

Sources indicate that humans and models also struggle in opposite places. People were least accurate on math and logic seeds. Models were strongest there and weakest on counting and reading text inside images.

Traders now hand AI tools real jobs: reading a contract, summarizing a token page, checking a wallet address in a screenshot, or running a bot. In those jobs, one wrong character or one miscounted number is the whole failure. A model that is right 19 times out of 20 will still be wrong on the 20th, and a signed transaction cannot be undone.

It has been revealed that 1. Ask twice. Run the same question more than once. If the answers differ, treat both as unconfirmed.

2. Check the visual parts yourself. Counts, colors, positions and text read from an image are where models slip most. Compare addresses and numbers character by character against the original.

Industry observers note that 3. Match the effort to the task. More reasoning helps with text and math. It helps little with images, so do not assume a longer "thinking" mode makes a screenshot read safe.

4. Keep a human on irreversible steps. Sending funds, signing transactions and changing settings should not rest on a single AI answer.

Zcash holders just got a new patch as the major crypto exchange Gemini has revealed support for Shielded Zcash deposits.

In a recent development, scott Merkel, 'Wolf of All Streets,' shared this update in an X post, highlighting the milestone as the first of its kind for any major exchange. According to Merkel, Gemini now lets customers deposit Zcash (ZEC) to shielded addresses, saying it is the first major exchange with both shielded deposits and withdrawals.

GEMINI NOW LETS CUSTOMERS DEPOSIT ZCASH $ZEC TO SHIELDED ADDRESSES, SAYING IT IS THE FIRST MAJOR EXCHANGE WITH BOTH SHIELDED DEPOSITS AND WITHDRAWALS https://t.co/d9pIFJ6uJM.

Gemini co-founder Tyler Winklevoss shared the milestone in a recent X post, adding that the recent move builds on the launch of shielded Zcash withdrawals on Gemini this summer.

In July 2026, shortly after the Ironwood upgrade was activated, Gemini launched support for shielded Zcash withdrawals to the fresh Ironwood pool, allowing customers to send Zcash from Gemini to their Ironwood deposit address. Ironwood (NU6.3) went live on July 28, 2026, at block height 3,428,143, bringing a new shielded pool for Zcash.

With the recent launch of support for Shielded Zcash deposits, Gemini owners can make Shielded Zcash deposits and withdrawals to and from Ironwood, with Winklevoss remarking that the private movement of money was now complete.

Zcash's total shielded supply now sits at around 4.93 million ZEC (around 28.94% of total ZEC supply) as of November 25, 2026.

Industry observers note that november has brought in key updates for the Zcash network. Zcash's NU7 upgrade went live earlier in November 2026, slashing ZEC's target block time to 25 seconds from 75 seconds. The upcoming 25-second block target lets miners add a batch of transactions to the chain three times as often.

Sources indicate that none of this prints extra ZEC. Each block pays a third as much and halvings come every 5,040,000 blocks instead of 1,680,000, so the issuance schedule holds at roughly four years per halving.

Days after the NU7 upgrade, the Zcash Foundation followed up with the release of Zebra 7.1.0, which fixed ten security advisories, most of which closed off ways in which another node on the network (a peer) could stop a Zebra node from catching up with the chain or make it run out of memory. It also added sync and memory diagnostics, automatic peer recovery, and clearer errors.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elon Musk called YouTuber Marques Brownlee “a chicken” early Saturday, hours after Tesla opened invite-only Cybercab orders at $29,990 and Brownlee argued that his famous head-shaving bet isn’t lost.

Tesla has about seven weeks to get a Cybercab into a customer’s hands for under $30,000 before 2027, but the half-baked version of Cybercab that they opened orders for with delivery in December makes it look like it’s just to win this dumb bet.

It has been revealed that surely Tesla isn’t down enough to deliver a half-baked product just to “prove” a YouTuber wrong? Or is it?

After Tesla’s “We, Robot” event in October 2024, Brownlee (MKBHD) remarked there was no way Tesla would deliver a Cybercab to a customer for $30,000 or less before 2027. If it did, he’d shave his head on camera.

Musk has taken it personally ever since. When the first Cybercab came off the Giga Texas line in February, he replied “Gonna happen 😂” to a bald-MKBHD meme, which we covered at the time. In September, after Brownlee doubled down in a latest video, Musk wrote: “I guess he really wants to shave his head 🤷‍♂️”.

On Friday, Tesla started inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use. The order page lists $29,990, a mandatory $299 per month Autonomy Subscription, a $1,000 non-refundable deposit, and an estimated delivery of December 2026, only in Tesla’s Texas Robotaxi cities.

According to recent reports, as we reported Friday, the car only operates inside Tesla’s Robotaxi geofences. And Tesla’s Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement states it “will not operate” without the $299 plan, bans owners from putting it on the Robotaxi network or using it for ride-hailing, and lets Tesla shrink the operating area at any time.

Sources indicate that so Tesla designed a robotaxi, then offered it to select private owners who aren’t allowed to use it as a taxi. Over five years, that’s $47,631 before insurance, registration, and charging. And you are limited to small geofenced areas. If you stop paying Tesla’s monthly fee, which it can change at all times, your cybercab becomes a paperweight.

Brownlee laid out his case Friday night. There are no deliveries yet, the car is invite-only rather than publicly available, and it can’t be used as a cab outside of the existing geofences. He called it “a paperweight if I take this thing home,” though he admits that last point isn’t technically part of the bet.

According to recent reports, the memes are everywhere, so let’s go back over the bet: Cybercab publicly available for under $30k by the end of 2026My hair is safe for several reasons1: No deliveries yet. But they’re estimating starting in December so that’s neat2: Invite only, not actually publicly… https://t.co/NCD2aFbe2c.

Tesla fans fired back with clips from his September video, where he described a car that “will not ship to regular people like you and me for $30k before the end of 2026.” Whole Mars Catalog, an Elon Musk propagandist whose real name is Omar Qazi, told him to “be a man and honor your word.” Musk reposted it, then replied:.

Musk also reposted a Grok answer claiming the current offer “matches” the conditions of the bet.

But around the same time, Musk replied directly to Brownlee’s post about the order page, and it didn’t help Tesla’s case:.

Sources indicate that “It will be available nationwide, as we receive regulatory approval. But the monthly fee is too high. Should match the cost of Tesla FSD and connectivity for other models, which is more like ~$115/month.”.

That’s Tesla’s CEO confirming, a day after launch, that the car can’t be sold outside the areas where it already operates and that its price is wrong. A price that Musk fully controls.

It has been revealed that yes, it looks like Tesla is rushing this out just to win a bet against a Youtuber. Absolutely insane behavior. We’ve seen this movie before. In June 2025, Tesla did a single “autonomous delivery” of a Model Y to meet a Musk deadline, then never did it again.

Tesla always pitched the Cybercab as a vehicle for its Robotaxi network. Now, seven weeks before the deadline, a personal-use version shows up that’s invite-only, Texas-only, banned from doing the one thing it was designed for, and attached to a subscription Musk himself says is too expensive. If you set out to build a product whose main job was letting Musk claim he won a Twitter bet, it would look a lot like this.

This Cybercab offering is completely broken. The value proposition is awful. As others have put it, it’s a permanent variable rate lease starting at $300 a month with a ridiculous $30,000 down payment.

Besides, the bet was "under 30k." Starting price is under 30k, but a subscription is required, which takes it over 30k, just to use it for one day. They could have given the car away for free, and just charged a fee to use it. Doesn't change the total cost.

Sources indicate that what do you get for this deal? A 2-seater vehicle that only works in small, incomplete, geo-fenced areas and has no steering wheel to do anything else with it. Meanwhile, Tesla insists that the Model Y, like the ones used in its current Robotaxi service alongside the Cybercab, uses the same self-driving technology.

Recent findings suggest that you can buy one for $40,000, and you get a lot more car than the Cybercab; then you can pay $99 a month for FSD instead of $300 a month. Tesla is supposed to let current Tesla owners drive without supervision in the geo-fenced areas, which would basically be the same product as what Tesla is offering right now with the Cybertruck, but you are not a slave to Tesla, which can brick your car at any time or change the terms.

This offer simply makes no sense, and Musk is sort of admitting it by saying the price should be the same as FSD, not $300 a month.

#157439. Why So Many Newly introduced Moms Are Told to Wait to Exercise Again—and What the Research Really Says

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1922 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Womenshealthmag ↗ Open Full Page

Why So Many Newly introduced Moms Are Told to Wait to Exercise Again—and What the Research Really Says

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1922 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Earlier this year, trainer and WH advisory board member Sohee Carpenter, CSCS, posted an Instagram Reel challenging some conventional postpartum advice: Don’t work out until your ob-gyn clears you at your six-week follow-up appointment.
  • “I feel like so many people get angry because they assume we mean you're going to be doing a one-rep max back squat a week after you have a baby,” Carpenter says.
  • It has been revealed that the problem, Carpenter explains, is that the six-week rule isn’t based on evidence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Earlier this year, trainer and WH advisory board member Sohee Carpenter, CSCS, posted an Instagram Reel challenging some conventional postpartum advice: Don’t work out until your ob-gyn clears you at your six-week follow-up appointment. Her point wasn’t that upcoming moms should rush back to the gym. It was that one timeline can’t fit everyone. Some women are ready to move sooner, and others need more time.

The Reel ruffled some feathers.

“I feel like so many people get angry because they assume we mean you're going to be doing a one-rep max back squat a week after you have a baby,” Carpenter says. “But that's definitely not what we're saying.” (By “we,” she means trainers who keep up with the latest research on pregnancy and postpartum exercise.).

It has been revealed that the problem, Carpenter explains, is that the six-week rule isn’t based on evidence. On the contrary, research suggests that this type of blanket advice doesn’t make sense for something as personal as postpartum recovery. When you return to exercise after childbirth should depend on your own symptoms, not a date on the calendar.

“There's really nothing magical about the six-week time point,” says Margie Davenport, PhD, a professor of kinesiology at the University of Alberta and chair of the 2025 Canadian Guidelines for Physical Activity for Pregnancy and Postpartum—the first-ever exercise guidelines to specifically focus on evidence-based suggestions for that first year postpartum. In the U.S., the main guidance from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) covers pregnancy and the postpartum period together. ACOG’s guidance points in the same direction, though: It says many women can start exercising again within days of an uncomplicated birth. In fact, “there is no identified ideal time to return,” Davenport says.

Sources indicate that based on the wide range of comments on Carpenter’s post—some supportive, some hypercritical, and still others asking more questions to try to better understand this shift away from the advice they’ve always heard—there’s still a lot of confusion around postpartum exercise. So we asked experts to break down what the research actually claims, and how to approach working out in this fresh chapter of life.

Industry observers note that in many cultures, the first 30 or 40 days postpartum is traditionally considered a protected time to rest, relax, and recover, Davenport says. In Chinese culture, it’s called zuo yuezi, which translates to “sitting the month.” In many Latin American and Latino communities, it’s known as “la cuarentena,” a nod to its roughly 40-day length. In South Korea, it’s sanhujori, or “postpartum care.”.

It has been revealed that these traditions carry deep cultural significance and are meant to offer real healing and support after birth from one’s community (they put “it takes a village” into practice). They’re rooted in caregiving and cultural custom, and they were never meant to serve as a medical timeline for when it’s safe to start exercising.

Recent findings suggest that in Western medicine, six weeks has become an crucial medical benchmark in postpartum recovery—and, over time, a default point for returning to exercise too. “At that point, your uterus should be back to its pre-pregnancy state, and so a lot of the gynecologic changes should be fairly reversed by that point,” says Rita Deering, DPT, PhD, associate professor of exercise science and director of the Pelvic Health, Exercise & Musculoskeletal (PHEM) Research Laboratory at Marquette University.

It has been revealed that the first six weeks after birth are also when the risk of complications like high blood pressure and infection is highest, Deering says, which is part of why that window became an important medical checkpoint (even though some pregnancy-related changes take longer to resolve). But, she says, “it was never intended to be about exercise.”.

Industry observers note that so how did six weeks become the exercise rule? Before researchers knew much about how safe it is to exercise during pregnancy and after birth, working out was considered potentially risky, Deering says. There wasn’t strong evidence that exercise wouldn’t slow healing or raise the odds of complications. So the most cautious advice was simply to wait until a doctor confirmed you’d healed enough to resume physical activity.

In a recent development, to come up with the 2025 Canadian Guidelines, researchers did a deep dive of all the available research on the topic, which included 574 unique studies organized into seven systematic reviews based on 21 different outcomes of postpartum exercise—such as depression and anxiety, low-back pain, injuries, glucose and blood pressure levels, and more. They also assembled an international panel of experts to give their recommendations.

Sources indicate that their advice: Start light-intensity physical activity and mobilization (think: carrying your baby around your home, a slow walk down the block, pelvic floor physical therapy) right away. From there, progress as you feel ready to moderate-to-vigorous activity such as brisk walking, resistance training, and running at your own pace—as long as tears and incisions have sufficiently healed and you don’t experience additional bleeding with exercise. (As mentioned, ACOG similarly recommends that women can return to postnatal exercise within days after an uncomplicated birth.).

Based on the research, there are no “absolute contraindications” to exercise postpartum, Davenport states—meaning no condition would rule out exercise entirely. There are some relative contraindications, she explains, “where you might have to delay a little bit or modify the type of activity that you're doing.” Examples include severe abdominal pain, extreme fatigue, and C-section incision pain that worsens with activity. All warrant a conversation with your doctor before starting.

In a recent development, want to Know More About Lifting While Pregnant? Start Here.

Pelvic floor symptoms, like leaking urine or a feeling of heaviness in the vagina, aren’t a reason to stop exercising altogether. If you notice signs of pelvic floor dysfunction, the guidelines recommend starting slowly and building up gradually instead. “Some leakage is okay,” Davenport states. “It means that the training that you’re doing is just overloading the muscle.”.

Recent findings suggest that many people, including plenty of commenters on Carpenter’s Reel, worry that exercising after birth will damage the pelvic floor and cause dysfunction. But the evidence doesn’t support that. In fact, those muscles will likely be better off if you resume training, especially if you do exercises to target them in particular. “Engaging in pelvic floor muscle training reduces your risk of urinary incontinence by around 37 percent,” Davenport claims. Additionally, if you stop all exercise because you're leaking a little bit, “this can actually mean that you're missing out on those other benefits.”.

One caveat: If you’re leaking a lot, or it’s getting worse over time, “you probably need to pull it back,” Davenport notes. That means being more selective about the moves you choose. For example, you might skip long runs and high-impact moves like jump squats for now, adds Sheridan Skye, a registered nurse, pre- and postnatal fitness coach, and founder of The Female Fitness Formula. Stick with lower-impact exercises, then build up gradually as you get stronger and your symptoms level off or improve.

Industry observers note that at the end of the day, every body, birth, and recovery is vastly different. “Some people have a very uncomplicated labor and delivery and pregnancy; for others, it's quite complex,” indicates Davenport. “It only makes sense that the way that they're returning and what time they're actually returning is also going to be quite individualized.”.

Recent findings suggest that for some newly introduced moms, six weeks is too soon, and a blanket deadline only adds stress. “Maybe they aren't sleeping or they don't have the support to be able to return [to exercise] at six weeks,” Davenport claims. On the flip side, for someone who had a straightforward delivery and is itching to get moving again, “telling them to wait for six weeks with no evidence to support it is also inappropriate.”.

According to recent reports, in fact, exercise can offer significant benefits during postpartum recovery, even before the six-week mark. “It improves muscle and bone density that we lose throughout pregnancy,” Skye states. Postpartum exercise is associated with a 45 percent reduction in the odds of developing postpartum depression, and starting before 12 weeks is even more beneficial.

According to recent reports, it’s also associated with a 28 percent reduction in the risk of developing diabetes postpartum. Exercise even improves sleep quality, Skye notes. “Women tend to feel more energized and like they've experienced more rest, even if they haven't,” she states. (Anyone who’s survived a 3 a.m. feeding stretch knows that’s no small thing!).

There is also evidence that exercise in general can help to decrease pain, states Deering, and research links sedentary behavior to lumbopelvic (the areas of the lower back and pelvis) pain. “So if you are having pain, movement might be what you need to help with that.”.

Sources indicate that for many people, it may be difficult to know if you’re truly ready. “Especially when you're postpartum, it can feel like you are super out of touch with your body sensations, especially if you're not sleeping well,” Carpenter says.

If you're at the point where you're thinking about it, but are nervous or unsure or just overwhelmed by having another decision to make, Davenport recommends taking the Get Active Questionnaire for Postpartum—a tool that her team designed as part of the 2025 guideline. It can help you quickly understand if you’re ready to start from a medical perspective. That can help give you some reassurance.

In a recent development, there can also be “a lot of fear involved,” Carpenter says, especially if you had a C-section or are healing from a vaginal tear. In that case, “you’re probably going to be a bit hesitant,” which is completely understandable. Starting slower and lighter than you think you need to is perfectly fine as you get reacquainted with your body. “The first several sessions are really about mentally trying to get that confidence back,” she says.

As you go, pay attention to how your body responds. Leaking, for instance? That’s not a reason to stop exercising, but you may want to adjust your workout to reduce it. More bleeding, newly introduced pain, or a sense that something just doesn’t feel right are signs to stop, reassess, and possibly scale back. If they don’t improve, check in with your doctor. “It’s really about setting your ego aside and being willing to modify, even if it’s one rep to the next, based on how you’re feeling right at that time,” Carpenter says.

It has been revealed that and if you feel physically ready but aren’t quite there mentally? “It’s okay to honor those feelings,” Deering says, “and to recognize that it’s okay to give yourself some time.” Whether that’s two weeks, six weeks, or six months, the right moment to start moving is the one that works for you.

Amy is a freelance writer and editor who covers health, fitness, and lifestyle topics—with a focus on practical advice that fits into real life. She previously worked as deputy fitness editor at SELF, and is both an ACE-certified personal trainer and a ProNatal pre and postnatal fitness specialist. Her work has been published in Women’s Health, Men’s Health, SELF, Wondermind, HGTV, Outside, REAL SIMPLE, The Upcoming York Times for Kids, and more. Amy lives in central New York where she spends her off-hours chasing after her two kids, digging into backyard gardening projects with her husband, and creatively squeezing at-home workouts into her schedule as often as she can.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Volkswagen revealed how much its new ID. Cross will cost, with prices starting at around $35,000 in the UK. But if you’re hoping to get the cheaper version, you’ll have to wait a bit longer.

After opening orders for the ID. Cross in Europe in July, Volkswagen is preparing to launch the entry-level electric SUV in the UK.

The ID. Cross is the all-electric equivalent of the T-Cross, Volkswagen’s smallest and most affordable SUV in Europe and the UK.

Following the ID. Polo, the ID. Cross is the latest from Volkswagen’s electric urban family of compact cars.

The electric SUV is 4,153 mm long, about the same length as the T-Cross, but its dedicated MEB+ platform offers more interior space. It seats five and offers a 475-liter boot, 20 liters more than the gas-powered T-Cross with the rear seats pushed all the way forward.

Sources indicate that when the rear seats are folded, the electric ID. Cross offers up to 1,345 liters of overall luggage volume.

Sources indicate that like in Europe, the Volkswagen ID. Cross will be available with two battery packs in the UK: a 37 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) pack and a 52 kWh nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) pack.

According to recent reports, the ID. Cross with the larger 52 kWh battery offers up to 265 miles of WLTP range, while the 37 kWh version provides up to 194 miles of WLTP range.

With DC fast charging of up to 105 and 88 kW, Volkswagen mentioned the vehicle’s battery can charge from 10% to 80% in as little as 23 minutes.

All versions are equipped with vehicle-to-load (V2L) capabilities, allowing it to be used as a mobile power bank for an e-bike, campsite, or other external electronic devices.

Inside, the ID. Cross adopts VW’s revamped interior digital cockpit design. Cross adopts VW’s revamped interior digital cockpit design. The setup includes a 10.25″ Digital Cockpit Pro instrument display and a 12.9″ infotainment screen. Based on driver feedback, Volkswagen brought back physical buttons for climate control and other vehicle functions.

Industry observers note that volkswagen will open orders for the ID. Cross Life and Style trims in the UK with the 52 kWh battery and 208 hp (211 PS) motor will go on sale on Thursday, November 19, starting at £30,260 ($40,000) and £33,675 ($44,500), respectively.

It has been revealed that the base ID. Cross Life and Style trims with the 37 kWh battery will go on sale in January 2027, with prices starting at £26,985 ($35,500) and £30,400 ($40,100).

Volkswagen said the 52 kWh version is eligible for the UK government’s £1,500 ($2,000) electric car grant. Eligibility for the 37 kWh versions is expected to be confirmed soon.

In Europe, Volkswagen opened orders for the entry-level ID. Cross Trend last month, starting at €27,995 ($31,000) in Germany, including VAT.

It has been revealed that as the electric counterpart to its popular T-Cross, Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer said the ID. Cross is “modern, reliable, and above all, affordable.”.

Recent findings suggest that sadly, VW has no prepares to bring the ID. Cross to the US. In early 2027, it will launch the new ID. Tiguan, which will replace the outgoing ID.4 SUV.

  • Latest data from the crypto analytics platform CryptoQuant demonstrates that about 4.61 billion XRP have flowed into crypto exchanges over the last 30 days.
  • According to the data, Binance has led all other crypto exchanges in the amount of XRP inflows received over the last month as its customers appear to have panicked amid rising market struggles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

XRP has continued to see traders deposit large amounts of tokens into exchanges, including Binance, Bybit and others, as the prolonged market volatility has triggered increased fear across the broader crypto market.

Latest data from the crypto analytics platform CryptoQuant demonstrates that about 4.61 billion XRP have flowed into crypto exchanges over the last 30 days.

According to the data, Binance has led all other crypto exchanges in the amount of XRP inflows received over the last month as its customers appear to have panicked amid rising market struggles.

As such, Binance recorded about 1.221 billion XRP deposits during the period, representing the lion's share of the total inflows.

Ranking second on the list is OKX, which followed with about 866.51 million XRP, while Bybit was next with 662.57 million XRP.

The trend extended to other exchanges, even though they saw considerably lower inflows: Upbit saw about 176.96 million XRP flow into its exchange during the same period, while Bitget recorded inflows of about 140.02 million XRP.

Although the past month has seen billions of XRP transferred back to exchanges, further data shows that the 4.6 billion XRP inflow is substantially lower when compared with inflows seen in October.

In October, the total XRP that flowed into exchanges throughout the month was estimated at around 6 billion XRP, suggesting that XRP selling pressure has eased compared with the previous month.

This has drawn attention across the crypto market as the price of XRP suffered larger losses this month compared with last month, sparking questions about whether investor confidence is recovering.

Sources indicate that morgan Stanley has disclosed its latest crypto-related holdings in a quarterly Form 13F filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. According to the filing, the bank's U.S. equity portfolio was valued at around $1.96 trillion as of Sept. 30, up from $1.89 trillion at the end of June.

Most of the crypto-related positions in the filing are Bitcoin products and Bitcoin-linked stocks, and the bank also reported a small amount of XRP exposure through three spot exchange-traded funds.

Industry observers note that the largest crypto-related position in the filing is Strategy (MSTR). Morgan Stanley held around 10.88 million MSTR shares worth about $1.67 billion at the end of September, up from 9.33 million shares at the end of the second quarter.

The bank also increased its position in BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) from 16.48 million to 19.52 million shares, and the IBIT stake was worth about $924 million as of Sept. 30.

Sources indicate that besides, Morgan Stanley reported 6.72 million units of its own Morgan Stanley Bitcoin Trust (MSBT), up from 2.57 million units at the end of June. In the second-quarter filing, the MSBT position was worth about $43.3 million. MSBT started trading on NYSE Arca in April, and it was the first spot Bitcoin ETF issued by a major U.S. bank.

Among crypto stocks, Morgan Stanley also held around 10.54 million Robinhood (HOOD) shares worth about $1.19 billion and 3.72 million Coinbase (COIN) shares worth about $694 million.

Morgan Stanley reported $116,097 in XRP ETF holdings as of Sept. 30. Franklin's XRP fund accounted for $111,885 of that amount, REX-Osprey's fund for $3,098, and the Bitwise XRP ETF for the remaining $1,114.

Industry observers note that the bank held the same three funds at the end of June. In the second quarter, Morgan Stanley reported 6,715 shares of the Franklin fund, 255 shares of the REX-Osprey fund and 67 shares of the Bitwise fund. Before that, the bank's first-quarter filing highlighted 1,700 shares of the Volatility Shares XRP ETF and 100 shares of the Grayscale XRP Trust ETF worth $15,488 in total.

On Wednesday, XRP was trading at around $0.908, down 2.23% over 24 hours, according to CoinMarketCap.

According to recent reports, morgan Stanley was one of seven banks that disclosed XRP-linked ETF holdings in third-quarter 13F filings. The positions of the seven banks totaled about $29.4 million as of Sept. 30, and Italy's Intesa Sanpaolo accounted for $27.21 million of that amount.

Goldman Sachs reported much larger XRP positions. The bank's XRP ETF holdings rose from $87 million in the second quarter to $144 million in the third quarter, and Goldman's crypto portfolio was worth around $2.64 billion in total.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that french senators on Nov. 24 rejected a proposal that would have required taxpayers to disclose self-hosted cryptocurrency holdings exceeding €100,000.

They would have had to report those assets as of Dec. 31.

This would have been the case even if they had held the same coins since January without making any sales.

Two matching amendments to the French 2027 budget were rejected by the Senate during the first reading of the draft.

Senators Pascal Savoldelli and Anne-Sophie Romagny reintroduced the proposal after it briefly passed in the National Assembly earlier in the month.

French taxpayers must disclose their crypto assets held on foreign crypto platforms.

In a recent development, these amendments would have expanded disclosure requirements to wallets that owners directly control. This pertains to a wallet that is not managed by an exchange or another custodian.

The French National Assembly approved the €100,000 disclosure threshold in a 150-44 vote on Nov. 3. There were also eight abstentions.

The next day, the National Assembly voted down the entire revenue portion of the budget.

This vote brought down the wallet disclosure provision along with the rest of the budget.

However, the subsequent effort to revive the provision in the Senate was defeated.

It should be noted that the 2027 budget is still being considered at the time of writing.

The Senate also rejected two other crypto-related measures debated as part of the budget.

One was a provision to tax gains realized when holders exchange cryptocurrencies for certain stablecoins.

The second was a proposal to expand France's exit tax to include unrealized gains on cryptocurrencies held by taxpayers who move their tax residence outside the country.

Shiba Inu (SHIB) kept leaving crypto exchanges this week as the price of the meme cryptocurrency fell to levels last seen in the spring of 2021, and on Wednesday, the outflow picked up sharply.

According to CoinGlass data, 520.83 billion SHIB left exchanges over the past 24 hours. That amount made up most of the 757.51 billion SHIB that exchanges lost over the past seven days, and over the past 30 days, the outflow reached 2.88 trillion SHIB.

In a recent development, on Wednesday evening, SHIB was trading at $0.00000344, according to CoinGlass. So far this week, the token was down 4.78%, and its market capitalization went down to $2.02 billion, according to TradingView.

According to the weekly chart on TradingView, SHIB last traded at these levels in the spring of 2021, months before the token reached its all-time high of $0.00008845 on Oct. 28, 2021.

Sources indicate that from early 2026 until mid-November, the price of SHIB held above $0.000004, and the yearly low stood at $0.00000411 at the July 17 close. In November, SHIB fell to $0.00000373, and in late November, the token dropped as low as $0.00000337. On Jan. 1, the token closed the day at $0.00000692, and since the start of the year, SHIB has lost 50.3% of its value, according to CoinGlass. As of Nov. 22, SHIB had lost 22.7% in November so far, according to CryptoRank.

Sources indicate that the latest drop in SHIB came after Bitcoin fell back below $60,000 this week. On Saturday, Nov. 21, Bitcoin dropped as low as $55,150, its lowest price since September 2024. Over the past 24 hours, $57,590 worth of SHIB futures positions were liquidated, and $54,750 of that amount came from long positions on OKX, according to CoinGlass.

The Wednesday outflow was not the first large one this month. On Nov. 17, about 312 billion SHIB were withdrawn from exchanges, according to CryptoQuant. On the same day, the number of SHIB holders on Ethereum passed 1.7 million, according to Etherscan.

It has been revealed that coinGlass data also shows that since late 2024, the total SHIB balance on exchanges has gone down by 19.18 trillion tokens, or 20.54%, to 74.19 trillion, and over the same period, the price of SHIB fell by 88.39%. The remaining 74.19 trillion SHIB on exchanges make up 12.59% of the circulating supply and are worth about $254.75 million.

Most of the 24-hour outflow came from exchanges that CoinGlass groups as "Others," as their combined SHIB balance fell by 88.5% to 70.93 billion tokens. Over the same period, the SHIB balances of Binance and OKX barely changed, and Coinbase, Bitfinex and Bitstamp added SHIB.

As a result, in the week when the price of SHIB fell to levels last seen in 2021, exchanges lost more SHIB in a single day than over the previous six days combined, according to CoinGlass data.

Tesla on Autopilot/FSD hit an overturned truck at 71 mph, killing 3

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1513 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A Tesla Model 3 drove into an overturned box truck on I-75 near Naples, Florida, killing two of its passengers and a man who had stopped to help.
  • According to recent reports, police and local media covered the May 31 crash as a truck wreck in the dark, and none of it mentioned a driver-assist system.
  • on Sunday, May 31, 2026, the 31-year-old driver of a 2014 Freightliner lost the road near the Pine Ridge Road exit in Collier County, steered back onto southbound I-75, and flipped it, according to the Florida Highway Patrol.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A Tesla Model 3 drove into an overturned box truck on I-75 near Naples, Florida, killing two of its passengers and a man who had stopped to help. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators states Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, at 71 mph.

According to recent reports, police and local media covered the May 31 crash as a truck wreck in the dark, and none of it mentioned a driver-assist system. It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data, and it lands as Tesla’s monthly crash count hits another record.

Just before 4 a.m. on Sunday, May 31, 2026, the 31-year-old driver of a 2014 Freightliner lost the road near the Pine Ridge Road exit in Collier County, steered back onto southbound I-75, and flipped it, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The overturned truck ended up blocking the center and outside lanes.

Recent findings suggest that jonathan Garcia Arias, a 25-year-old Naples man and former Marine, was driving by in a BMW. He pulled over and got out to help the truck driver.

It has been revealed that then a southbound 2023 Tesla with five young men from Naples inside came up on the scene. FHP’s report notes the front of the Tesla hit the underside of the overturned truck and Garcia Arias. Two of the Tesla’s passengers, aged 18 and 19, died at the scene, and Garcia Arias died later in the hospital. The 20-year-old driver and two more passengers were seriously hurt.

In a recent development, A few days later, FHP used the crash as a warning about stopping near wrecks on the interstate. Senior Trooper Kenn Watson said the Tesla driver would have seen only the truck’s underside, with “no lights, no reflectors, nothing warning them.”.

So that’s the official story. A dark obstacle, a driver who couldn’t see it in time. Nobody stated a word about Autopilot.

In a recent development, under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone was killed or hurt. Tesla filed one for this crash.

It has been revealed that it identifies the car as a 2023 Model 3 on a highway, flags a traffic incident on the roadway, and marks the automation “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged.” That means Tesla confirmed through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 71 mph and a fatality, lists the Florida Highway Patrol as the investigating agency, and claims it learned of the crash from police and the media.

Then it blacks out the crash narrative, the software version, and whether the road was within the system’s approved operating domain, all as “confidential business information.” That’s the same redaction Tesla applies to 99.9% of its reports.

The report also surfaced late. Tesla filed it as a 5-Day report, the urgent category for fatal crashes, but it didn’t land until Tesla’s September filings, more than three months after the crash. And Tesla lists law enforcement as one of the ways it found out about it.

Recent findings suggest that how we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 07:56 UTC, which converts to 3:56 a.m. in Florida, two minutes off the 3:54 a.m. in FHP’s report. The city, the highway, the 2023 model year, the month and the fatal outcome all line up, and it’s the only fatal Tesla driver-assist report in Naples that month. It’s the same crash.

Recent findings suggest that A Tesla on driver-assist going highway speed into the underside of a big truck, in the dark, in Florida. If that sounds familiar, it should.

In 2016, Joshua Brown was killed near Williston when his Model S on Autopilot drove under a tractor-trailer crossing the highway. In 2019, Jeremy Banner died in Delray Beach when his Model 3 on Autopilot went under a trailer at 68 mph and had its roof sheared off. In both crashes, neither the driver nor the system braked.

In a recent development, trooper Watson’s point was that a human couldn’t see the truck. But a significant, unlit obstacle sitting across two lanes at night is exactly the kind of thing a driver-assist system is supposed to catch, and Tesla now sells FSD as nearly ready to drive with nobody watching. And an attentive driver could clearly see it, as the BMW driver did, and stop before the Tesla arrived.

According to recent reports, we want to be fair about what the data doesn’t prove. “Engaged within 30 seconds” is the reporting trigger. Tesla’s 71 mph may be a telematics snapshot rather than the impact speed. And with the software version redacted, we can’t say whether this was Autopilot or FSD.

Sources indicate that the NHTSA release that surfaced this crash, covering filings through October 15, also set a new monthly high. Tesla reported 264 driver-assist crashes in September 2026, beating July’s 236, which was itself a record. That’s up from 135 in March.

September may still grow as late reports come in. This Naples crash shows how late they can be.

Our merged dataset now holds 4,669 Tesla driver-assist crash reports since 2019, 69 of them flagged fatal. The same release added two other fatal reports, both “Verified Engaged” and both covered locally with no mention of driver-assist: a Model Y that hit a tree and burned in El Dorado Hills, California, killing three, and a Model X that hit a signal pole in Naples on September 30, killing a passenger. We’ll lay those out separately.

In a recent development, three people died on I-75, including a man who got out of his car to help a stranger. Tesla knows its driver-assist was on, knows the speed, holds the telematics, and filed a federal report saying so. Then it sealed everything that would explain what the car did, and the public got a story about a dark truck.

Recent findings suggest that that's what happens when the system has to identify all objects in the camera frame before it can start to estimate the objects position and then relative distance and then relative velocity. Unrecognizable objects will destroy all your logic. This is a design failure and not something Tesla can actually fix.

Sources indicate that compare that to radars and lidars that directly measure distances and relative velocities of everything in front of the car, regardless of what it is. That is a far better approach because you do not want the car the impact objects on its trajectory regardless of what those objects turn out to be.

According to recent reports, tesla’s whole pitch for FSD is that the car sees better than you do, and yet, Tesla vehicles on Autopilot and FSD keep crashing on stationary objects on the highway. It’s the same failure that killed Joshua Brown and Jeremy Banner years ago. If the system saw the truck and the driver overrode it, Tesla should say so. It was quick to do that in the Katy crash when the data helped it. If the system didn’t see it, that’s a safety defect regulators and owners need to know about.

In a recent development, either way, the redaction protects Tesla, not the people on the road. It’s the same pattern we found in Vineland and in July’s four fatal crashes, and the crash count keeps setting records.

Recent findings suggest that we’re asking the Florida Highway Patrol for the full crash report, whether its investigators got Tesla’s raw vehicle data, and whether they even knew the system was engaged. If they didn’t, the only party that knows what this car did is the one that sealed the file.

The Franklin Crypto Index ETF is preparing to add Hyperliquid to its portfolio, according to a prospectus supplement filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on Wednesday.

The fund right now holds Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP, Dogecoin, Solana, Cardano and Stellar.

The HYPE token will be held in spot, with its allocation determined by its weighting in the underlying CF Benchmarks index. The fund is expected to maintain a portfolio structure broadly aligned with the index.

The move comes as major trader Abraxas Capital reportedly exited its Hyperliquid position on Wednesday. The firm is said to have generated approximately $530 million in profits from the trade.

In September, Hashdex added HYPE to its Nasdaq CME Crypto Index ETF, with a 3.36% weighting.

It has been revealed that currently, there are three Hyperliquid ETFs: THYP and HYPG by 21Shares, and Bitwise's BHYP. Their combined assets, however, remain relatively low, currently under $259 million.

Hyperliquid is trading near $59.8, down 1.3% over the past 24 hours and 10.2% over the previous week.

According to recent reports, the $55-$56 range is an immediate support area. A move above $60 could signal declining selling pressure, while a decline below the range could lead to more liquidations and further correction.

HYPE has slipped below its major moving averages, including the 200-day moving average near $68, reinforcing the bearish outlook.

Meanwhile, the RSI hovers around 35, indicating weakening momentum and approaching oversold conditions.

The market is also preparing for an vital token unlock scheduled for Dec. 6. Reports estimate that the release could be worth $578 million at current prices.

Case in point: My go-to headphones for strength training at the noisy gym are different from what I reach for when it comes to HIIT and running.

No matter the style and fit you prefer, elements like sweat resistance, battery life, sound quality, and adjustability are crucial, too. And, while I love a good bargain, I’ve learned that you can’t just grab any random pair of cheap headphones or earbuds and expect them to do the job well. After multiple rounds of testing, these are the best wireless workout headphones to consider.

The Apple AirPods Pro have always been a reliable pair of headphones for me, and the latest third generation is even better. Whether I’m biking or struggling through heavy reps, it delivers a premium experience, including impressive sound and a comfortable fit. And the latest edition further proves their God-tier status: heart rate, step, and calorie tracking.

It has a sensor that deciphers your pulse through your ear canals, which then calculates calories burned based on heart rate. I like to keep tabs on my heart rate during high-intensity cardio, so it’s a great alternative to wearing a fitness tracker. Just make sure the fit is right to get an accurate reading (four silicone ear cup sizes are available).

Industry observers note that it also has motion sensors that can track your steps. All data transfers to the Apple Health app, so you need to own an iPhone or iPad. Luckily, I recently converted (sorry, Android).

According to recent reports, when I’m grinding hard at the gym, I want to hear nothing around me except my hype house music. The active noise cancellation drowns out any grunters, loud gym music, TVs, and general unnecessary background noise. I feel like it’s just me and my music, so that I can laser-focus on the task at hand.

But when I need to maintain awareness during outdoor runs, I turn on transparency mode to hear oncoming traffic and people nearby. I also like that it automatically lowers my music when it detects me talking to someone. It has an IP57 rating, meaning it’s sweat and dust-resistant, and can be submerged in a meter of water for up to 30 minutes in case of any accidental puddle drops (been there). As someone who sweats a lot, each bud repels moisture very well and doesn’t fall out of my ears when jumping or running. Plus, sweat never clogs my ears—something I experienced with regular AirPods. The ear cups are made from a lightweight material that feels breezy against your ears, minimizing extra sweating while you work out.

In a recent development, these headphones also have an impressive battery life of 40 hours, which is only second on our list to the Powerbeats Pro 2. Skullcandy clearly designed these headphones for convenience, with plenty of buttons within easy reach. As a result, you can swiftly turn the volume up or down without missing a beat. If active noise cancellation is a must for you, scroll up—while the sound quality on these headphones is excellent, they won’t help you fully tune out the world.

It has been revealed that the Skullcandy Crusher 540 headphones don’t have an official IPX rating, but they have a special sweat- and water-resistant nano-coating to protect your gear. (The ear cup pads are also removable for easy cleaning.) A major draw of these headphones is the strong bass, which comes in handy during tough workouts. As someone who loses nearly everything, I appreciate the built-in Tile technology to help you find your headphones with the Tile app if you misplace them.

According to recent reports, I first tested the Bose Open Ultra Earbuds last fall, and they’ve been my favorite pair for distance running ever since. These earbuds aren’t going anywhere thanks to a design that’s similar to a clip-on earring. Just gently hook these on your ears and move on. The style is perfect for people like me who have been burned in the past by an earbud falling out and vanishing forever.

As an early morning runner who regularly crosses streets, I appreciate the open-ear audio these earbuds deliver. I can hear my music perfectly, but still can detect things like chirping birds to give me a solid awareness of my surroundings. You can adjust the volume, skip songs, and flip between immersive and stereo sound with a tap on your earbuds, making it easy to switch things up mid-run.

A heads up: If you’ve never used an earbud style like this in the past, you may need to give your ears a little time to build up to wearing them. My ears were a little sore when I first started wearing the Open Ultra Earbuds, but I don’t even feel them when they’re on now. These earbuds are also IPX4 rated for water resistance, so they do just fine with light splashes or rain—just make sure you don't wear these to swim laps.

Recent findings suggest that the earbuds have a seven-hour battery life, which is lower than several others on this list. But I’ve never had an concern with them dying on me. I just pop them in their charging case when they’re not in use.

It has been revealed that some people are going to struggle to get earbuds to fit, no matter what they do. If you have smaller ears and you’re over flipping through different ear tips in hopes something will fit, the Beats Powerbeats Fit are a solid choice. These earbuds actually fit inside your ears like a hearing aid with the help of flexible wingtips that really lock them in there.

These earbuds are small, but they deliver the top-tier sound quality you’ve come to expect from Beats. That includes the options to flip between active noise cancellation and transparency modes, so you can use these to tune out loud gym-goers or to be aware of your surroundings during outdoor workouts.

According to recent reports, these earbuds pair seamlessly with Apple and Android phones, making them an equal opportunity headphone. They also have an IPX4 rating for sweat and splash resistance, so you can wear them in the rain, but not to swim laps. While the Powerbeats Fit comes with four different tips, your ears will still need a little time to get used to these before wearing them on, say, a 10-miler.

According to recent reports, the earbuds do kind of jam in there, and it can take some time to get used to the feel of the wingtips. But if you’re looking for a discreet pair of headphones that aren’t going anywhere, you can stop your search here.

In a recent development, if you want secure earbuds that aren’t an investment, the Anker Soundcore Sport X20 fits the bill. It costs a third of the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 and shares the same ear-hook design that doesn’t budge when pushing your limits during high-impact workouts. The sound is shockingly premium given the $80 price tag. If I were doing a blind test, I’d think it costs at least $200.

Industry observers note that the strong noise cancellation blocks out every peep imaginable at the gym. From loud gym music to weights slamming, I can’t hear a thing except my jams. But when I don’t want to be super locked in, I switch to “normal” mode so I can listen to background noise. This mode is handy when running or walking at night. And when things get too wet during intense grinding sessions, the IP67 sweat-resistance saves me. Although I haven’t tested it while swimming, it can withstand water submersion beyond one meter for about 30 minutes.

Sources indicate that the silicone ear hooks are soft, flexible, and extremely comfortable. I find myself reaching for it outside of the gym and often forget it’s even on my ears, which I’m not mad about—it makes a great cool-girl accessory. The only downside of wearing it for too long is that the battery will drain after about eight hours. Luckily, the charging case has two days' worth of battery life—so no excuses to skip a workout.

The Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 are my go-to for long-distance running because of the wrap-around and open-ear design that stays in place. It’s no surprise it’s a TikTok-viral favorite among runners and our editors.

In a recent development, the sweat-resistance rating is one notch below our best overall, with an IP55 score, meaning it can withstand intense rain during rough outdoor conditions. Moisture from sweat is never an concern since the design hangs over the ear and doesn’t go in the canal. It even alerts me with a vibrating beep if moisture is present in the port while charging.

If blocking out noise is your priority, you should consider other options, as this pair doesn’t offer noise cancellation. I don’t love that I can’t be fully engaged in my music, but that’s the trade-off for running safely. Unlike other headphones I tested in this guide, the sound emits outside of the eardrum using bone conduction technology, which is when noise is transmitted through vibrations in the skull to reach the ear. I hear every sound, from people talking to traffic, so I give it a perfect score for maintaining awareness. I deem it an essential pair if you train early in the mornings or at night. Just note it’s not going to be the same listening experience as the Apple AirPods Pro 3, for example.

The battery life is nowhere near the capacity of the Apple AirPods Pro 3, with only about 12 hours of playtime, so I find I have to charge it weekly for an hour. The flip side is that it only takes 10 minutes to get two hours of battery life if I quickly need it before a run.

Sources indicate that full disclosure: They come in two sizes, but tend to run large, which is why I went with the mini size. I ordered the standard size first and had to return them (small head probs).

If you plan on running, spinning, or doing other high-intensity training, it’s best to have headphones that can withstand sweat. They should have an IP rating, which is a protection score for how well electronics can resist water. “IPX4 or higher is perfect for working out,” claims Joe Smith, an audio specialist at Music Critic. All options on this list have at least an IPX4 rating.

But our best budget option, the Anker Soundcore Sport X20, has an even better score of IP67, meaning it can handle being submerged in just over one meter of water for 30 minutes. If headphones aren’t made to withstand sweat, it’s best to reserve those for lower-intensity workouts.

According to recent reports, having your headphones die during a half-marathon is not the vibe (been there). Using a pair with good battery life is crucial to ensuring the tunes are always going strong during a long workout. With select pairs, it can be dependent on whether or not select features are in use.

It has been revealed that for example, the total playtime for the new Apple AirPods Pro 3 from a single charge (with case) is up to 10 hours with active noise cancellation turned off, but only up to eight hours with it turned on. Carl Prouty, a tech expert at Abt, recommends snagging a model that charges fast in case you forget to plug them in the night before.

Noise cancellation is a function that utilizes a microphone hidden inside the earbud or earcup to analyze frequencies that emit opposite sound waves, thus helping to reduce background noise. Blocking out surrounding noise is great for staying focused and immersed, but it’s not the safest feature in desolate areas like quiet trails, busy streets, or at night.

I prefer an open-ear style to maintain awareness during outdoor runs. If you’re not a fan of that design, other options on this list allow you to turn noise cancellation on and off. “If you still want to be able to hear what's going on around you while also listening to music, look for a model with a good ambient and pass-through mode,” says Prouty.

According to recent reports, you have a lot to choose from in a workout headphone, and each has its pros and cons. Earbuds rest inside your ears to deliver sound without bulk. These tend to fit comfortably, but may pop out if you don’t get the fit right. Ear hook earbuds add an extra layer—a hook that goes over your ears—to help combat this problem. There are also open-style headphones that hook over your ears and around the back of your head to keep them in place.

A newer category of these is open earbuds that clip over your ear like a clip-on earring, while nestling into your ear like an earbud. Finally, over-ear headphones have soft cups that fit over your ear for a classic look. While these usually do a good job staying in place, they may feel hotter during intense workouts than other designs.

It has been revealed that as a distance runner, I rely on good music to keep me hyped up and entertained on long runs. I’ve tested dozens of pairs of wireless headphones for working out over the past decade and learned what features make pairs stand out. Only workout headphones with good sweat resistance, battery life, noise cancellation, and sound transparency made the final cut.

Because everyone has different needs in a workout headphone, I also leaned on experiences from Women’s Health editors, along with Men’s Health senior gear and reviews editor Ryan Brower. Each pair was used in different environments during cardio and strength training sessions to see how they performed when put to the test during workouts. Those included 5- to 10-mile runs, indoor cycling workouts, HIIT sessions, and more general lifting at the gym.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Andrew Webley, CEO of The Smarter Web Firm, mentioned that Bitcoin's drop has been sharper than he had anticipated, but he does not think the digital asset's price will decline much further.

The British CEO, whose company recently added 55 BTC to its treasury, remarked investors' opinions on Bitcoin can shift considerably without any changes to Bitcoin itself.

"Sentiment towards Bitcoin can change very swiftly. Without Bitcoin changing at all," Webley remarked on X.

It has been revealed that webley advised investors to consider Bitcoin's movements relative to other assets. Bitcoin's price decline highlights investors how much the cryptocurrency has lost in absolute terms.

However, Bitcoin's performance relative to the broader market may indicate BTC is being sold specifically or whether investors are taking profits across multiple markets. Webley did not specify which assets he was comparing Bitcoin against.

"Do I expect Bitcoin to go significantly lower from here? No. But as the past few weeks have shown, predicting short-term price movements is a very challenging task," Webley said.

Some of the most challenging periods for investors, he said, were followed by some of his most profitable periods.

His most definitive prediction concerned Bitcoin's longer-term outlook: "Bitcoin has an incredible future.".

In fact, Webley's tech giant has been buying more Bitcoin as its price has been dropping.

On Nov. 17, Smarter Web mentioned it spent around £2.75 million on 55 BTC, bringing its total holdings to 2,905 BTC.

The average purchase price was £49,991 per Bitcoin, roughly 38% below the treasury's overall average purchase price of £81,234 following the transaction.

Smarter Web borrowed around £2.6 million under its Coinbase credit facility to finance most of the purchase. The company used its existing Bitcoin holdings as collateral.

Following the transaction, Smarter Web had around £19 million outstanding under the dollar-denominated credit facility.

The rebound comes after sharp swings triggered by leadership uncertainty, concerns over AI infrastructure spending and tighter US chip export controls.

It has been revealed that broader US futures are also pointing higher, suggesting the recovery extends beyond Nvidia. However, the latest rise faces an crucial test: whether buyers can sustain momentum after the stock’s recent reversal or whether the rally will fade as investors reassess risks surrounding the AI trade.

Industry observers note that nvidia shares rose approximately 3.6% in premarket trading on November 27, according to market data. The move followed a sharp decline on Wednesday, November 25, when NVDA closed at $149.30, down 3.91%, after touching an intraday low of $141.17.

BREAKING: Nvidia $NVDA is up almost 5% in pre-market on rumors that the US government could buy a stake in the manufacturer.President Trump also stated he will speak to Jensen Huang soon. pic.twitter.com/b1UHHgVwtT.

The recovery is part of a broader rebound across US technology stocks. Nasdaq 100 futures advanced more than 2% as investors returned from the Thanksgiving holiday, while S&P 500 and Dow futures also moved higher. Semiconductor companies, including AMD and Broadcom, joined the advance.

In a recent development, black Friday brings a shortened US trading session, with exchanges scheduled to close at 1 p.m. ET rather than the usual 4 p.m. The holiday shopping event also places consumer spending in focus, although retail sales are not the direct catalyst for Nvidia’s premarket move.

Nvidia’s recent volatility has been closely linked to the reinstatement of co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO on November 23. The announcement triggered a historic rally, with shares jumping more than 31% in a single session before reversing part of the gains over the following two trading days.

President Donald Trump said he had spoken with Nvidia’s board and helped secure Huang’s return. Trump has also indicated that he plans to speak with Huang, while raising the possibility of a US government stake in Nvidia. However, no government investment agreement has been declared.

Industry observers note that leadership uncertainty is only one part of the challenge. Nvidia is also facing scrutiny over its China-related business, export-control compliance and the economics of the broader AI infrastructure boom. The reported pause in AI server shipments to four Southeast Asian countries has added another layer of uncertainty for the company and its manufacturing partners.

Industry observers note that investors will also be watching upcoming congressional scrutiny involving Huang. His return has eased one immediate leadership concern, but it has not resolved the regulatory and governance questions surrounding the tech giant.

Nvidia shares closed near $149.30 after falling as low as $141.17. The stock price has broken below its previously marked demand zone and remains under pressure from declining moving averages. The latest premarket rebound towards the $155–$156 region offers an initial recovery signal, but buyers need to reclaim nearby resistance before the broader technical structure improves.

The first hurdle is around $155–$157. A sustained move above this region could bring the $160–$165 area into focus, which is crucial after the sharp reversal from the recent rally. On the downside, $149 remains an immediate reference level, while the $141 area marks the recent intraday low.

The Black Friday session may provide an early indication of whether investors are willing to rebuild positions in Nvidia. However, lighter holiday trading volumes can make price movements less reliable.

A sustained recovery will require stronger buying beyond the initial premarket reaction. For now, NVDA’s nearly 4% premarket gain signals renewed interest in the AI trade, but the manufacturer’s export restrictions, leadership scrutiny and broader AI investment concerns remain unresolved.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • "Bitcoin investors tend to sell BTC when there's a massive IPO.
  • That's Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong's take on Bitcoin investor behavior, less than a week after the record-breaking $93.5 billion IPO of Claude creator Anthropic.
  • Industry observers note that "Historically, people rotate out of it to take advantage of a big IPO.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"Bitcoin investors tend to sell BTC when there's a massive IPO. Then they come back.".

That's Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong's take on Bitcoin investor behavior, less than a week after the record-breaking $93.5 billion IPO of Claude creator Anthropic.

Industry observers note that "Historically, people rotate out of it to take advantage of a big IPO. Then they come back in," Armstrong wrote on X earlier today.

The limited window of opportunity to invest in an IPO helps explain the behavior Armstrong described. For an investor to buy at the IPO price, there's only a certain period during which they can request an allocation of shares. After that, the price is determined by the market.

In a recent development, on Nov. 19, Anthropic went public on the Nasdaq, and that brief window of opportunity mattered.

Industry observers note that shares were priced at $83, up from the $70-$78 range indicated just two days earlier. Anthropic's stock, trading under the ticker ANT, opened at $111.50.

If you bought at that opening price, you paid about 34% more per share than an investor who received an allocation at the IPO price.

When the IPO closed on Nov. 20, 1.127 billion shares had been sold, including 147 million additional shares purchased by underwriters exercising their option.

Recent findings suggest that of the $93.5 billion in gross proceeds, Anthropic itself received around $91.6 billion. The rest went to existing shareholders.

It has been revealed that there was also a separate $26 billion private placement involving investors such as Microsoft, Nvidia, Google and others. In total, the combined transactions were valued at $119.5 billion.

As for the longer-term case for holding BTC, Armstrong's point concerns investors' expectations about the future purchasing power of their money.

"If you think there is going to be more inflation and money printing in the future, bitcoin is as notable as ever.".

At the heart of the matter is Bitcoin's 21 million supply limit.

According to recent reports, if you expect governments to continue expanding the money supply, you may still be excited by the prospect of a major IPO. And you may sell some of your BTC to participate in it.

Armstrong's argument is that the window of opportunity to participate in a major IPO eventually closes.

However, the reasons investors bought Bitcoin in the first place may remain long after the newly listed stock starts trading.
